title: Star-shaped Dynkin trees T_{x,y,z}: det(Cartan) = xyz(1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1)
connection: The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n.
why: Brings in lattice/root-system tools (discriminant groups, Vinberg reflectivity) and the recent weighted-star-tree classification of Torrente-Lujan.
first_step: Compute discriminant groups of T_{x,y,z} lattices for ES triples of small p; see whether they have a uniform structure (e.g. cyclic of order xyz(n−4)/n).

title: Weighted star trees with central weight k: determinant xyz(k − 3 + Σ 1/x_i) — ES with integer offset
connection: Torrente-Lujan allows central diagonal entry k; the determinant becomes xyz(k − 3 + 1/x + 1/y + 1/z) (k = 2 recovers xyz(Σ 1/x_i − 1); e.g. k = 3, arms (2,2,2) gives 12). Different k shift the target by integers, giving 'ES with integer offset'.
why: Integer offsets are trivial arithmetically but the matrix world might impose inertia/definiteness constraints that select ES-relevant triples.
first_step: Read arXiv:2605.23011 for the determinant formula with general k and record the induced Egyptian equation.

title: Spherical / Euclidean / hyperbolic trichotomy as a 'phase diagram' of numerators
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z > 1 (spherical: the infinite family (2,2,r) plus finitely many others), = 1 (Euclidean: (3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)), < 1 (hyperbolic). ES with 4/n < 1 sits in the hyperbolic regime; numerators m/n > 1 give the spherical lists.
why: The classification for sums > 1 (one infinite family plus a finite list) is the archetype of an 'Egyptian classification' theorem; ES is the infinite hyperbolic regime where no classification is possible but density is.
first_step: Record as context; check whether 'which rationals in (1, 3] are 3-term sums' (finite-ish lists per denominator) gives a useful contrast for heuristics.

title: Tessellations and Wythoff constructions: uniform tilings with vertex configurations from ES triples
connection: A triangle (π/x, π/y, π/z) tiles the hyperbolic plane; vertex/edge/face counts of Wythoff tilings depend on 1/x+1/y+1/z. ES triples give tilings with angle defect 2π·... proportional to (1 − 4/n).
why: Mostly a reformulation; potential value is visual/heuristic (e.g. counting tilings with given defect).
first_step: Low priority: note equivalence; compute angle defects of ES triangles for p ≤ 100.

title: Hypergeometric differential equations: exponent differences 1/x, 1/y, 1/z with Σ = 4/n
connection: Schwarz's list: the hypergeometric equation with exponent differences (λ, μ, ν) has monodromy a triangle group when they are reciprocals of integers; λ + μ + ν < 1 gives hyperbolic monodromy. ES ⇔ some Schwarz triangle with reciprocal angles has angle sum 4π/n.
why: Connects to monodromy/arithmetic of hypergeometric functions (Beukers–Heckman); ES triples give specific hypergeometric families whose arithmeticity could be tested.
first_step: Context; check whether any ES triple gives an arithmetic monodromy group (overlaps Takeuchi item).

title: Toric/polytope view: ES triples ↔ reflexive-like triangles with given lattice data
connection: A lattice triangle with vertices on axes at distances x, y, z (simplex with intercepts) defines the plane X/x + Y/y + Z/z = 1, which contains the diagonal point (t,t,t) iff Σ 1/x_i = 1/t. So ES ⇔ some plane with positive integer intercepts passes through (n/4, n/4, n/4).
why: Lattice-point/geometry-of-numbers view: find a lattice plane with positive integer intercepts through the diagonal point at height n/4. This is a 'plane through a point' problem amenable to geometry of numbers.
first_step: Formalize: planes with integer intercepts through (t,t,t), t = n/4; parametrize by normal vector (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) and relate to the repo's lattice forms.

title: Lattice of solutions: the Z-span of solution vectors (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) as p varies
connection: For each p the solutions give rational vectors with coordinate sum 4/p. Their Z-span or the lattice generated by the denominators across p might show hidden linear relations (e.g. always containing a fixed vector).
why: A fixed vector in all solution spans would be a 'universal certificate' in disguise.
first_step: Compute for p < 2000 the lattice generated by (lcm/x, lcm/y, lcm/z) and look for invariants.

title: Lens-space/Seifert covering maps as transport between ES(n) and ES(dn)
connection: A d-fold fibre-preserving cover of the Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) multiplies e(M) by a factor depending on how fibres unwrap; for unwrapping that keeps β_i = 1 one gets ES-type equations for other n.
why: If covers map ES(n') solutions to ES(n) solutions with n' | n or n | n', it is a topological composition law; combined with an inductive scheme it would give ES for products.
first_step: Work out Euler numbers of covers of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres (Jankins–Neumann formulas).

title: ES as an integer-programming feasibility problem: divisor enumeration per p; flatness ideas need a convex relaxation
connection: For fixed p, ES is the feasibility of a small polynomial system over Z; after fixing the Type (I/II) and parameters it reduces to divisor enumeration (factorization), so ES is easy per p in practice; Lenstra/Kannan (fixed-dimension LINEAR integer programming) do not directly apply to these quadratic constraints.
why: If a slice can be relaxed to a convex body whose integer points are solutions, Khinchine's flatness theorem (lattice width) could force a point — this needs a genuinely convex formulation, which the quadratic slices lack.
first_step: Formulate one Type II slice as a lattice-width question; compute the width for hard primes and see whether Khinchine's flatness bound could force a point.

title: Thick object: the multiplicative group (ℤ/pℤ)^× and its subgroup lattice
connection: ES certificates for p correspond to residues of p modulo many 4ad, but one could also look mod p: x ≡ ? mod p. The set {x : 4x ≡ … mod p} is 'thick' (size p); extraction rule: lift to ℤ with size constraints.
why: Generator-matrix item (thick object × extraction rule): (ℤ/p)^× as thick object with an archimedean extraction rule.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a condition on a residue mod p plus a size bound and check whether the residue set has structure (subgroup/coset).

title: U failures factor as products of small primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) and one larger factor
why: Composite U failures are driven by the composite structure (factors ≡ 3 mod 4 make n+v divisors in the needed class scarce?); 25305 contains 241 (least p ≡ 1 (4) with least QNR 7) — a weak link to pseudosquare-type hardness.
first_step: Test whether U-failure rate among n ≡ 1 (8) depends on the number of prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4) of n; predict further failures beyond 10⁹ from that profile.

title: Sibling 4/n with denominators in an arithmetic progression or geometric constraints
connection: Solutions with y − x = z − y or y² = xz (geometric) are 'rigid' sub-families; their existence sets at primes are new exception sets.
why: Rigid families are where polynomial-identity constructions live; their failure sets indicate which residue classes each rigid family covers.
first_step: Add the two flags to the variant counter and list failures at primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: Distribution of x/p over all solutions (the 'x-profile')
connection: Histogram of x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4] over all solutions at primes 10⁴–2·10⁵; expect mass near 1/4 (greedy) with a 1/(4x − p)-type law.
why: The x-profile is the density a sieve over x must reproduce; deviations (e.g. secondary peaks at x/p = 1/3, 1/2) show identity families.
first_step: Extend the count program to histogram x/p and y/p.

title: Balanced solutions (z ≤ 10x) frequency
connection: Fraction of primes with a solution having z/x ≤ C for C = 10, 100, 1000; BALANCED_LATTICE.md studies balanced points.
why: If balanced solutions exist for all large p with C fixed, geometry-of-numbers on the cubic surface (bounded-height points) would suffice — a strong statement to falsify cheaply.
first_step: Add a min z/x statistic to the count program and record its maximum over p ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Near-isosceles solutions: smallest y − x (or z − y) at p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since x = y is impossible at p ≡ 1 (4), the minimal gap y − x over solutions is a fingerprint of how close the hard class comes to the degenerate locus.
why: If the minimal gap is always small (bounded or ≪ log p), near-degenerate families might give uniform certificates.
first_step: Add min(y − x) and min(z − y) to the count program; tabulate at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Primitive projective triples
connection: View denominator triples as rational points up to common scaling, with p recovered from their reciprocal sum.
why: Scaling explains why prime cases are central and may separate shape from arithmetic size.
first_step: Enumerate primitive triples with coordinates below 100 and sort the resulting reduced values of 4xyz/(xy+xz+yz).

title: Denominator ratios as slopes
connection: Parameterize y/z by a reduced rational slope and express the ES condition in terms of its numerator and denominator.
why: A rational slope organizes triples differently from fixing x and might reveal short covering families.
first_step: Derive the divisibility condition for y=ku,z=kv with gcd(u,v)=1.

title: Bilinear determinant encoding
connection: Represent uv−r as a two-by-two determinant and translate ES divisor conditions into determinant equations with congruences.
why: Determinants bring row operations and lattice bases into a directly arithmetic setting.
first_step: Write a residual factor-pair certificate as a determinant condition and list congruence-preserving row operations.

title: Fundamental domain boundary crossings
connection: Follow a moving residue target through lattice fundamental domains as p changes and record when short representatives appear.
why: Boundary crossings may explain abrupt changes in the cheapest certificate.
first_step: Track nearest lattice representatives for consecutive admissible primes in one explicit two-variable model.

title: Ehrhart families of auxiliary polytopes
connection: When a parametrization reduces to linear inequalities and congruences, study its integer-point count as the bounds dilate.
why: Quasipolynomial counts can give exact finite-family information without addressing nonlinear cases automatically.
first_step: Isolate one linear parameter region and compute its first several dilation counts.

title: Inside-out polytopes for exclusions
connection: Represent linear positivity regions with forbidden congruence hyperplanes or boundary subspaces in a lifted lattice.
why: This separates the bulk feasible region from thin degeneracies.
first_step: For a small linear family, list forbidden hyperplanes and count remaining lattice points at low dilation.

title: Discrete Morse reductions
connection: Assign a combinatorial gradient to a bounded certificate complex and collapse redundant regions.
why: A reduced complex might isolate the essential obstructions to moving between certificate families.
first_step: Build a small complex from compatible local moves and test elementary collapses with explicit free-face checks.

title: Nerves of parametrization charts
connection: Construct the nerve whose vertices are exact parametrizations and whose simplices record shared certificates.
why: Intersections may expose a small core of identities linking otherwise separate approaches.
first_step: Compute pairwise and triple intersections for five small parametrization families over a finite prime sample.

title: Star–triangle arithmetic moves
connection: Test the electrical star–triangle transformation as a source of rational three-variable identities with controlled denominator factors.
why: The network equality is exact, but integer preservation needs explicit extra conditions.
first_step: Write the star–triangle formulas and solve their integrality requirements for small positive integer inputs.

title: Convex relaxations of bounded searches
connection: Relax selected bilinear constraints using valid convex envelopes inside a finite parameter box.
why: The relaxation can prune impossible boxes or reveal promising corners, without supplying integer witnesses by itself.
first_step: Apply McCormick envelopes to one bounded auxiliary equation and compare feasible boxes with exact enumeration.

title: Reciprocal convexity bounds
connection: Use convexity of 1/t to derive necessary bounds on denominator sums and imbalance within a chosen search region.
why: These bounds are elementary and can reduce search without risking false sufficiency claims.
first_step: Derive Jensen and tangent-line bounds for ordered x≤y≤z satisfying the reciprocal sum.

title: Harmonic–arithmetic mean constraints
connection: Relate denominator spread to the fixed reciprocal sum through mean inequalities.
why: Quantitative spread bounds can distinguish balanced and highly skewed certificate families.
first_step: Derive the sharp lower bound on x+y+z over positive real solutions and inspect the integer gap for small p.

title: Stationary points of certificate cost
connection: Minimize smooth proxies such as log(xyz) on the real ES surface under specified denominator ordering and bounds.
why: Critical points indicate where an integer search should concentrate, not where integer solutions must exist.
first_step: Use Lagrange multipliers for one bounded cost and compare its minimizers with actual small certificates.

title: Curvature-adapted sampling
connection: Sample near the real solution surface with density adjusted to local curvature and rounding sensitivity.
why: This may propose integer candidates more efficiently than sampling a rectangular box.
first_step: Compute the Hessian of z=pxy/(4xy−p(x+y)) and compare two bounded sampling schemes.

title: Hidden-number-style parameter recovery
connection: Treat partial information about modular products as a lattice recovery problem for an auxiliary parameter.
why: The analogy is meaningful only when the available information matches an explicit hidden-number instance.
first_step: Write a toy recovery problem with exact known high bits and compare its recovered parameters with valid certificates.

title: Logarithmic geometry of denominator exclusions
connection: Treat denominator vanishing loci as a marked divisor and compare charts respecting that divisor.
why: A log-geometric description may organize which coordinate changes preserve the relevant open set.
first_step: Write the marked boundary for two birational charts and compute how each boundary factor transforms.

title: Motivic comparison as a bookkeeping lead
connection: Ask whether several auxiliary varieties share a common geometric decomposition that explains repeated finite-field count formulas.
why: A decomposition could transfer exact counting identities, but any motivic interpretation remains to be checked.
first_step: Compute point counts of two related charts over several small odd fields and seek an explicit cut-and-paste decomposition.

title: Finite-field incidence bounds
connection: Represent a reduced certificate relation as incidences between points and curves over a finite field.
why: Incidence geometry can estimate modular witness abundance, with integer lifting kept as a separate problem.
first_step: For the residual factor equation modulo q, identify the point and curve sets and count incidences directly for small q.

title: Hyperbolic lattice-point counting in a 'thin' cone: ES as a Selberg-pretrace positivity
connection: ES's Type II condition ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a 'determinant = 1' condition on a 2×2 integer matrix [[f, 2c], [2cd, f′]]... (up to normalization); counting such matrices with congruence constraints is hyperbolic lattice point counting.
why: Lattice-point problems in SL₂(ℤ) have error terms via spectral theory; the campaign's B3 says the main term is only log²p, but spectral *positivity* (not counting) might still apply to a cleverly weighted sum.
first_step: Verify exact matrix form: find integers such that det [[f, α],[β, f′]] = 1 encodes ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 (α β = 4c²dp); then check whether the congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd is a Γ₀/Γ₁-type condition.

title: Topological-insulator-style 'bulk-boundary' invariant: Mordell classes as a bulk, squares as the boundary
connection: The 6 square classes mod 840 are the 'boundary' where polynomial identities fail; a ℤ/2 invariant (Brauer class) separates bulk from boundary. Bulk–boundary correspondence predicts protected 'edge states' — here, solutions that exist for a reason that only works away from squares.
why: Pure analogy, but it gives a design principle: look for mechanisms indexed by a ℤ/2-valued invariant that is nontrivial exactly on non-squares (e.g. a Jacobi symbol (p/m) that is +1 at squares).
first_step: List all ℤ/2 invariants of the form 'Jacobi symbol of p w.r.t. something determined by (C,d)' that are identically +1 when p is a square, and check which the known Type I/II identities use.

title: Möbius inversion on the divisor lattice (Rota) for the certificate indicator: express 1[∃ a | N, a ≡ −1 (m)] via Möbius function of the lattice of divisors
connection: The event 'some divisor lies in a class' is a union over divisors; inclusion–exclusion on the divisor lattice gives an exact alternating formula; the 'Möbius algebra' of the divisor poset might simplify when the class condition is a character condition.
why: Exact combinatorial formula alternative to the character-sum formula; may expose cancellation structure.
first_step: Write the formula for N squarefree with ω factors (2^ω terms) and compare its complexity to the character formula (φ(m) terms); use whichever is smaller per regime.
refs: Rota, 'On the foundations of combinatorial theory I'

title: Unit-fraction Tilings: Egyptian squares (Rédei-style tiling by rectangles of area 1/n)
connection: Tiling a rectangle by rectangles of sides 1/a×1/b relates to Egyptian decompositions ↔ ES as a 3-piece tiling of a 4×p-ish rectangle.
why: Tilings give geometric invariants (Dehn-type) that sometimes prove impossibility or existence.
first_step: Formulate: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ tiling of a (4·lcm)-strip; check if any Dehn-like invariant is non-trivial.

title: Toric degenerations and Ehrhart counting of ES solutions in boxes
connection: Counting lattice points in polytopes defined by Type II inequalities ↔ Ehrhart quasi-polynomials.
why: The (★) count over a cut-off region is a lattice-point count in a hyperbolic region; Ehrhart theory with dilation p might give exact periodic formulas for partial counts.
first_step: Restrict to u ≤ U, B ≤ V and count solutions mod 4uB to p as function of p; check if it's a quasi-polynomial in p of bounded period.

title: Lattice reduction geometry: ES as short vector in a p-dependent lattice of bounded dimension
connection: Repo has lattices L_ρ; Minkowski's theorem gives short vectors pointwise ↔ need vector in a prescribed coset/positive cone.
why: Minkowski is pointwise (T-type size squeeze); the question is whether some lattice of determinant ≍ p has a short vector that is automatically a certificate.
first_step: List repo lattice forms; for each compute Minkowski's guaranteed short vector length vs certificate size bound.

title: Crystallography / Bravais lattices: 1/x+1/y+1/z as Miller-index relation
connection: Miller-index plane equations x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 ↔ the plane through (x,0,0),(0,y,0),(0,0,z) contains the point (p/4,p/4,p/4) ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some lattice plane with positive integer axis intercepts passes through (p/4)(1,1,1). Lattice-plane counting (geometry of numbers) might apply.
first_step: Use this: count lattice planes through q = (p/4)(1,1,1) with integer intercepts; relate to primitive vectors (1/x,1/y,1/z) scaled — check if this is a known equivalence to ET.

title: Factoring with hints: ES as 'find a factor of 4Cp+1 in a residue class' (Coppersmith known-MSB/LSB attacks)
connection: Coppersmith factors N given half the bits of a factor; ES wants a factor of N_C = 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C — i.e. the low bits (mod 4C) of the factor are known.
why: Known-LSB factoring (factors in a prescribed class mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}) is polynomial time via lattices; ES's modulus 4C is tiny relative to N^{1/4}, but summing over C gives many tries.
first_step: Quantify: for which C is 4C ≥ (4Cp+1)^{1/4}? (C ≥ p^{1/3}) — then Coppersmith decides existence of a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C exactly; check whether the large-C range alone has certificates often (data).

title: Lattice attacks on 'hidden number problem' as a model for finding u with p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1)
connection: HNP: recover hidden α from approximations of α·t mod q ↔ ES conditions as simultaneous approximations.
why: Cryptanalysis has fine-tuned lattice dimensions/bounds for such problems; reuse could design efficient certificate finders for huge p.
first_step: Write ES Type II as approximations of p/(4uC−1) to integers; try a BKZ-based search for certificates at p ~ 10^40 and compare yield with brute force.

title: Learning-with-errors / lattice duality analogy: no
connection: LWE hardness vs ES certificate search ↔ superficial: both involve modular linear relations.
why: Probably vacuous; kept low confidence as a pointer that lattice duality (transference) could convert 'no certificate' into 'short dual vector' — a dual certificate of failure.
first_step: Formulate: if no certificate in lattice coset, transference gives a short dual vector; compute dual vectors for (★)-failing p = 409 and see if they look structured.

title: Borsuk–Ulam / necklace splitting as existence via equivariant topology
connection: Necklace splitting existence via Borsuk–Ulam ↔ ES as fair division of something?
why: Curiosity; equivariant topology proves existence without construction (PPA-type).
first_step: Look for a ℤ/2-equivariant map whose zeros are ES certificates (e.g. using symmetry y ↔ z).

title: Geometry: ES as a lattice point on a hyperboloid-like surface in 3D and Minkowski–Hlawka counts
connection: Positive solutions (x,y,z) lie on a smooth surface in ℝ³ (cubic) ↔ counting lattice points on surfaces near the asymptotic directions (where one coordinate dominates).
why: Lattice points on curved surfaces: counts ≍ area / curvature-weighted; ES surface's curvature degenerates at infinity — where solutions concentrate.
first_step: Compute the 'area' of the ES surface patch in the box [p/4, p²]³ weighted appropriately and compare with log² p — a geometric derivation of the main term.

title: Dimension theory: Hausdorff dimension of p-adic limits of failing primes (if infinitely many)
connection: If infinitely many (★)-failures existed, their closure in Ẑ is a compact set ↔ its dimension measures 'how sterile'.
why: Gives a quantitative profinite object for (★) failures (which are known to exist: 14 ≤ 10¹⁰); compare with sterile set K.
first_step: Compute residues of the 14 (★)-failing primes mod small moduli and see whether they lie in a small profinite set (e.g. all squares mod 3·5·7·…).

title: Sangaku (Japanese temple geometry) problems with unit-fraction radius relations
connection: Many sangaku give relations like 1/√r = Σ 1/√r_i or 1/r = Σ 1/r_i for tangent circles ↔ ES as an integer-radius configuration.
why: Curiosity/outreach; a configuration with 1/r = 1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/r3 among mutually tangent circles might connect ES to Descartes/Apollonian integrality.
first_step: Search sangaku collections (Fukagawa–Rothman 'Sacred Mathematics') for a three-reciprocal radius relation and check if it's Descartes-compatible.

title: Categorification: R(p) as dim H⁰ of a complex whose Euler characteristic is explicit
connection: If certificates span H⁰ of a natural complex (e.g. Koszul complex of the divisibility conditions) with χ = explicit positive quantity and H¹ small, existence follows ↔ Euler-characteristic arguments in algebraic combinatorics.
why: Speculative but concrete: Euler characteristics are exact and often computable from local data — an R-type input.
first_step: Write the Koszul complex for the ideal (4uC − 1)·k − (p + u) over a polynomial ring truncated by degree bounds and compute its Euler characteristic numerically for small p.

title: Ehrhart / lattice points on dilated segments: N(p; u,B) as an Ehrhart quasi-polynomial value
connection: The denumerant N(n; u,B) counts lattice points on the segment {ux + By = n, x,y ≥ 0} — a rational polytope; its Ehrhart quasi-polynomial has period uB ↔ ES(★) ⟺ for some (u,B), the quasi-polynomial at n = p hits the 'minimal' constituent.
why: Ehrhart reciprocity relates N(n) and N(−n − u − B) (interior points); p = 4CuB − u − B means −p − u − B = −4CuB: the Ehrhart reciprocity partner of p is a multiple of uB — a crisp algebraic restatement of the (★) condition.
first_step: Verify via Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity: N(p) relates to the interior count at 4CuB; derive (★) ⟺ 'p's reciprocity partner is divisible by 4uB' and check numerically.

title: Rigidity reading: 3 cone points (triangle groups) are rigid, 4 cone points have moduli — mirrors 3-term ES hard vs 4-term easy
connection: Teichmüller space of S²(x₁,…,x_k) has dimension 2k − 6: zero for triangle groups, positive for 4 or more cone points ↔ ES with 3 terms is hard while the 4-term analogue is easy.
why: A heuristic link between geometric rigidity and arithmetic sparsity (polylog solutions). It suggests looking for 'deformation' arguments that start from a 4-cone-point solution (always available) and degenerate a cone point (order → ∞ or merging) to reach 3 points.
first_step: Write the degeneration: 4/p = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d with d → merging (1/c + 1/d = 1/e) — count how often a 4-term solution has two terms merging to a unit fraction (same as batch A's 4→3 collapse item; check the geometric version gives anything new).

title: Weighted projective line: ES(★) ⟺ O(p) ≅ ω ⊗ π*O_{P¹}(4C) on the stacky curve P(u,B)
connection: On P(u,B) one has h⁰(O(n)) = N(n; u,B) (denumerant), ω = O(−u−B), and O(uB) = π*O(1) from the coarse P¹ ↔ p = 4C·uB − u − B is exactly deg(ω) + 4C·deg(π*O(1)).
why: Puts (★) into algebraic-geometry language where Riemann–Roch/Serre duality on stacky curves is the Popoviciu formula and the denumerant symmetry N(n)+N(g_t−n) = t is Serre duality. Type I might then correspond to stacky curves with three orbifold points — a uniform geometric home for both types.
first_step: Verify the Serre-duality derivation of N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on P(u,B); then test whether Type I certificates correspond to line bundles of the form ω ⊗ (pullback) on P(a,b,c)-type stacky curves (three orbifold points).

title: Torus knots T(u,B): 2g(T(u,B)) = (u−1)(B−1) and the (★) relation p + 1 = 2g + (4C−1)uB
connection: The semigroup ⟨u,B⟩ is the semigroup of the plane-curve singularity x^u = y^B (link = torus knot); its conductor is 2g = (u−1)(B−1) ↔ (★): p = 4CuB − u − B ⟺ p + 1 − 2g(T(u,B)) = (4C − 1)uB.
why: Links (★) to singularity theory (Milnor number μ = 2g) and knot invariants (Alexander polynomial exponents = semigroup); speculative, but singularity theory has deformation/adjacency structures that might act on certificates.
first_step: Check the identity and ask whether the condition '(p + 1 − μ) ≡ 0 mod uB with quotient ≡ 3 mod 4' has a meaning for the Milnor fibre or for the Alexander polynomial evaluated at roots of unity.

title: Polyhedral/tiling vertex equations as Egyptian equations: classification precedents
connection: Vertex-configuration equations of tilings (e.g. Σ 1/k_i = const for polygons meeting at a vertex) are Egyptian-fraction equations solved by finite enumeration ↔ ES is the same algebra with an n-dependent right side.
why: Shows ES as 'a tiling-vertex equation at curvature 4/n'; mostly orientation, but hyperbolic tiling enumeration software could enumerate ES-type configurations quickly.
first_step: Write the angle condition for three regular polygons at a vertex of a hyperbolic tiling with prescribed angle defect and relate to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n.

title: Strong symmetric genus spectrum (May–Zimmerman: every value occurs) as a ∀g∃G sibling via triangle groups
connection: May–Zimmerman: there is a group of every strong symmetric genus. Proofs use explicit group families acting with triangle signatures; Riemann–Hurwitz ties genus to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (see triangle-orbifold item). Shares F01, F12.
why: A solved ∀∃ statement whose witness lives in the same unit-fraction equation (via Riemann–Hurwitz) — possibly a source of explicit families (x,y,z) with constrained 1/x+1/y+1/z.
first_step: Read May–Zimmerman's construction and check which signatures (x,y,z) and areas arise; see if area (p−4)/p is ever forced.

title: Hurwitz 84(g−1) / the spectrum of 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z: gaps near 0 vs ES's values (n−4)/n
connection: The set {1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z} has the minimum positive value 1/42 and a well-studied accumulation structure (Hurwitz). ES asks whether every (n−4)/n belongs to {1 − Σ1/x_i} (n ≥ 5).
why: The order structure of the triangle-group 'area spectrum' (it is well-ordered with known limit points) is classical; ES is a membership question for an explicit sequence in it.
first_step: Compute the area spectrum up to denominator 10⁶ and its intersection with {(n−4)/n}; visualise where the hard n sit in the spectrum.

title: Guth–Katz polynomial partitioning for real ES solution geometry
connection: Polynomial partitioning bounds incidences in ℝ^d; ES solutions are lattice points on the real cubic surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Upper bounds on lattice points near the surface across many n bound pair correlations of f(n).
first_step: Bound #{(n, x,y,z) : n ≤ N} incidences with the one-parameter family of surfaces via partitioning and compare with known Σ f(n)² ≍ N log^? estimates.
refs: Guth–Katz, On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Kontorovich–Nakamura crystallographic packings ↔ ES integral geometry
connection: Kontorovich–Nakamura classify crystallographic sphere packings via integral Lorentzian reflective lattices; ES has lattice/quaternion reformulations and a cubic integral surface.
why: Packing local-global problems (Apollonian) are the main family with proved reciprocity obstructions akin to T1.
first_step: Check whether any ES lattice L_ρ (LATTICE_MEETING.md) is a reflective Lorentzian lattice.
refs: Kontorovich–Nakamura, Geometry and arithmetic of crystallographic sphere packings, PNAS 116 (2019)

title: Discretised projection (Bourgain) / Furstenberg sets (Ren–Wang) for p-adic or real ES geometry
connection: Bourgain's discretised projection theorem and Ren–Wang's Furstenberg set resolution give sum-product in ℝ at scale δ; ES solution ratios (x:y:z) live on a real curve family.
why: Could bound concentration of solution directions, relevant to size-window (FORCED_WINDOW) statements.
first_step: Express the set of normalized ES solutions (x/n, y/n, z/n) as a δ-discretised set and test projection-dimension statistics numerically.
refs: Ren–Wang, Furstenberg sets estimate in the plane, arXiv:2308.08819
Bourgain, The discretized sum-product and projection theorems, J. Anal. Math. 112 (2010)

title: Type II as SL₂(ℤ) matrices with prescribed off-diagonal product (hyperbolic lattice counting)
connection: ff′ − ab = 1 with ab = 4c²dp: Type II certificates are integer matrices of determinant 1 with diagonal ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) and off-diagonal product fixed — a hyperbolic lattice-point problem in Γ(4cd)-cosets.
why: Spectral counting in congruence subgroups (Selberg 3/16, Kim–Sarnak 7/64) applies; the fixed product ab is a 'divisor-split' constraint.
first_step: Count matrices in a coset of Γ(4cd) with |entries| ≤ T and ab = 4c²dp numerically, compare with the spectral main term.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002)
Kim–Sarnak, appendix to Kim, Functoriality for the exterior square of GL4…, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira joint equidistribution of integer points and their orthogonal lattices
connection: AES prove joint equidistribution of primitive integer points on spheres together with the shape of their orthogonal lattice; ES certificates carry both a 'point' (solution) and an associated lattice (L_ρ).
why: Joint equidistribution could say the ES-relevant lattice shape is generic, so short vectors in cones (ES) exist for most representations.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice L_ρ at p as the orthogonal lattice of a vector and check whether AES's setup matches.
refs: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points on spheres and their orthogonal grids, arXiv:1411.1272
Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points and their orthogonal lattices, arXiv:1502.04209

title: Blomer–Harcos hybrid subconvexity for effective ternary representations
connection: Blomer–Harcos give hybrid subconvexity for twisted L-functions, enabling effective representation results for ternary forms (with Siegel caveats); ES's ternary analogues would need such input.
why: Effective bounds combined with 10^18 verification are the only way a ternary route could close a range.
first_step: Quantify the size beyond which Blomer–Harcos yields representations, for the discriminants arising in any ES ternary reformulation.
refs: Blomer–Harcos, Hybrid bounds for twisted L-functions, J. reine angew. Math. 621 (2008)

title: Siegel–Rogers mean value / random-lattice model for ES lattices L_ρ
connection: Siegel's mean value theorem and Rogers' higher moments give the distribution of lattice-point counts in random lattices; ES(p) ⟺ some lattice L_ρ(p) has a vector in a cone (LATTICE_MEETING).
why: A random-lattice model predicts P(no vector in cone) and its p-dependence — a cleaner heuristic than divisor lotteries.
first_step: Compute covolume and cone volume for L_ρ(p) and compare empirical 'empty cone' frequency with Rogers' Poisson prediction.
refs: Rogers, Mean values over the space of lattices, Acta Math. 94 (1955)

title: Browning–Vinogradov effective Ratner for SL(2,ℝ)⋉ℝ² (gaps in √n mod 1) for affine ES lattices
connection: Browning–Vinogradov make Ratner equidistribution effective on ASL(2) to count affine-lattice events; ES Type I/II with a fixed shift (p) are affine-lattice problems (L + p·v).
why: Affine lattices capture the inhomogeneous p-dependence that homogeneous equidistribution misses.
first_step: Formulate the ES certificate set as points of an affine lattice in a region and check the BV setup.
refs: Browning–Vinogradov, Effective Ratner theorem for SL(2,R)⋉R^2 and gaps in √n modulo 1, J. LMS 94 (2016), arXiv:1311.6387

title: Hyperbolic circle problem in Γ₀(N) for e-slice counts
connection: Counting Γ₀(N)-orbit points in hyperbolic discs has spectral asymptotics with error controlled by exceptional eigenvalues; e-slice certificates ab | N with a ≡ −b (mod e) can be phrased via matrices with lower-left entry divisible by e.
why: Moves the e-slice count into a standard spectral counting problem.
first_step: Construct the matrix encoding of e-slice certificates and count numerically vs Γ₀(e) disc-count predictions.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002), ch. 12

title: LLL / Coppersmith small roots for ES Type I certificates at fixed p
connection: Coppersmith's method finds small roots of modular polynomials; Type I asks for f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd), a small-root problem for a polynomial in (c,d) modulo an unknown divisor (Howgrave-Graham variant).
why: Turns certificate search into lattice reduction with provable size ranges; complements factoring-based search at 10^18–10^25.
first_step: Implement Howgrave-Graham's 'approximate common divisor / unknown divisor' lattice for N(c) = p² + 4c²d, d fixed, and compare its hit rate with brute force at p ~ 10^20.
refs: Coppersmith, Small solutions to polynomial equations, and low exponent RSA vulnerabilities, J. Cryptology 10 (1997)
Howgrave-Graham, Approximate integer common divisors, CaLC 2001

title: OAI 182 power savings for polynomial differences at primes (claimed)
connection: OAI 182 claims power-saving Sárközy-type bounds for differences P(p), p prime; ES certificate polynomials evaluated at primes are a polynomial-at-primes family.
why: Weak link; records that difference-set methods at prime arguments now have power savings.
first_step: Check whether any ES certificate condition is a 'difference set avoids P(primes)' statement; likely close.

title: Linking form of the double branched cover of a 2-bridge link with a 3-vertex plumbing description
connection: L(p,A) is the double branched cover of the 2-bridge link b(p,A). The ES₅ sign is the isometry class of the linking form of Σ₂(b(p,A)), and HJ length 3 means a 3-vertex linear plumbing (negative-CF) description. Note this is not an 'even' continued fraction: three even HJ digits would give an even determinant.
why: Knot theory has exact formulas tying linking forms, Goeritz matrices and signatures (Gordon–Litherland). If σ mod 8 detects (A/p), the ES sign becomes a knot signature on a 3-parameter knot family.
first_step: Compute σ(b(p,A)) by Murasugi's formula Σ_{i<p} (−1)^{⌊iA/p⌋} for p < 500. Check whether σ mod 8, together with p mod 8, determines (A/p) (a van der Blij / Gauss-sum reciprocity).
refs: Gordon–Litherland 1978, On the signature of a link

title: Heegaard Floer d-invariants of L(p,A) as an obstruction/selector for 3-chain plumbings
connection: d-invariants of lens spaces satisfy an explicit recursion (Ozsváth–Szabó), d(L(p,q),i) via d(L(q, p mod q), j). Plumbing length 3 constrains the negative-definite fillings, and the ES sign is the homotopy class.
why: d-invariants are a native tool for deciding which lens spaces bound which definite 4-manifolds (Lisca's rational-ball classification itself used Donaldson's theorem and lattice embeddings; d-invariants give complementary obstructions). They might give a closed-form test of 'some 3-chain filling exists in the non-square class'.
first_step: Implement the Ozsváth–Szabó recursion. For p < 2000, compare Σ_i d(L(p,A),i) statistics over the classes A with r(p/A) = 3 between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Rational balls bounded by lens spaces (Lisca) vs 3-chain plumbings
connection: Lisca classified lens spaces bounding rational homology balls (p = m², specific q). Square p is exactly where ES-type certificates vanish (T1), and rational-ball bounding is tied to the linking form being metabolic.
why: T1 (obstruction at odd squares) and 'bounds a rational ball' are both 'linking form is split/hyperbolic' phenomena. A Lisca-style lattice-embedding argument could explain T1 topologically and show why primes escape it.
first_step: Read Lisca math/0701610 §§2–3 (lattice embeddings). Check whether the T1 square-class obstruction is equivalent to the metabolic linking form of L(m², A) for the relevant A.
refs: arXiv:math/0701610 (Lisca, Lens spaces, rational balls and the ribbon conjecture)

title: Lattice embedding of the 3-chain into the diagonal lattice ℤ^k (Donaldson-style)
connection: If a definite filling can be glued to another definite filling (of the reversed manifold) to give a closed definite 4-manifold, Donaldson's theorem forces the combined intersection lattice to be diagonal, so the plumbing lattice embeds in −ℤ^k (Lisca's method). For the chain (v,t,u), embeddings into ℤ^3 or ℤ^4 are explicit combinatorics, and the ES sign is a property of the complement lattice's discriminant.
why: This is the native toolbox of 4-dimensional topology for lens spaces, and it turns ES₅ into a finite combinatorial embedding question at each p.
first_step: Enumerate embeddings of chain lattices with det p into ℤ⁴ for p < 500; check whether the orthogonal complement's discriminant square class equals the ES sign.

title: Toric surface with three boundary curves: HJ-length-3 cones as compact toric surface data
connection: A 2-dim cone of type 1/p(1,A) whose resolution has 3 rays corresponds to a toric surface patch. ES₅ asks for a smooth fan refinement with 3 new rays whose self-intersections (−v,−t,−u) give p, with a twist class.
why: Toric geometry turns the condition into lattice-polygon combinatorics (Oda's 12/24 theorem for complete fans), which might give global constraints linking different A's.
first_step: Write the 3-ray refinement condition as a lattice-polygon statement; check whether completing the fan to a compact toric surface forces relations between v, t, u and A (mod 4).
refs: Oda, Convex bodies and algebraic geometry (1988)

title: Goeritz matrix of an alternating 2-bridge diagram equals the chain matrix
connection: For the plumbing description, the Goeritz form of a suitable 2-bridge link diagram should be (up to sign and stabilisation) the tridiagonal chain matrix (check the diagram convention: plumbing digits are not the same as twist-region counts of the standard diagram). Gordon–Litherland gives σ = sign(G) − μ.
why: This pins ES₅ to an explicit knot diagram: a 3-twist-region 2-bridge knot of determinant p. Knot tables could be scanned for the sign.
first_step: Check against KnotInfo: for 2-bridge knots with det p ≡ 1 (4), p < 200, and 3 twist regions in even CF form, record the linking-form class.

title: Quantum (WRT) invariants of lens spaces: Gauss sums carrying (A/p)
connection: Jeffrey's formula for the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant of L(p,q) involves Dedekind sums and quadratic Gauss sums whose evaluation produces Jacobi symbols in q. The ES sign may appear as a phase of a quantum invariant of L(p,A).
why: Quantum topology has exact formulas (and quantum modularity results) for WRT invariants of Seifert/lens spaces. A sum over words of a quantum invariant could be a computable object.
first_step: Write τ_r(L(p,A)) (Jeffrey 1992). Check whether some level r makes the phase equal to (A/p), and evaluate Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p)} τ_r(L(p,A)).
refs: L. Jeffrey, Chern–Simons–Witten invariants of lens spaces and torus bundles (CMP 1992)

title: Hyperbolic triangle billiards / Veech triangles with prescribed area
connection: Billiards in the hyperbolic (π/x, π/y, π/z) triangle unfold to the triangle group's tiling of H² (not to Euclidean translation surfaces). Separately, Euclidean rational triangles unfold to translation surfaces, and Veech's lattice triangles are special shapes there. ES is a statement about the area spectrum of reflection-group triangles.
why: A genuine dynamics translation of the original equation, but probably only a restatement. Recorded for breadth.
first_step: Check whether the area/angle condition has any known role in Veech-group classification (Kenyon–Smillie, Ward triangles).

title: Ford circles: A/p lies in a horoball of 'depth-3' chain
connection: r(p/A) = 3 means the Ford circle chain from ∞ to A/p has three tangency steps of HJ type. ES₅ becomes: some non-residue A has A/p inside the union of depth-3 Ford horoball chains.
why: The Ford circle picture makes the condition a covering-by-horoballs statement, where hyperbolic volume arguments live.
first_step: Draw/compute the union of depth-3 HJ horoball chains intersected with {A/p}; measure its proportion and its correlation with QR.

title: Closed geodesic of γ_w on the modular surface: trace N−m and word length 3
connection: γ_w is hyperbolic when |A+A*| > 2. Its closed geodesic has a cutting sequence of length governed by the word. Prime geodesic theorems with Jacobi-symbol twists (Sarnak's class-number sums) count such objects.
why: Prime geodesic theorems in conjugacy classes and with characters are fully developed; ES₅ is a twisted count of geodesics with very short cutting sequences.
first_step: Write trace(γ_w) = tu + tv − 2 = A + A* and list the conjugacy classes; check whether ES₅ is equivalent to a short-cutting-sequence geodesic of trace in a given set with a character condition.
refs: Sarnak, Class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms (1982)

title: Toric degeneration of U_n to the torus complement xyz ≠ 0 and the Newton polytope
connection: As n varies, 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) degenerates (n → 0, n → ∞) to toric strata. Newton polytope methods (Bernstein–Kushnirenko, Khovanskii) count solutions in tori over finite fields; positive integer solutions relate to the polytope's interior lattice points.
why: Newton-polytope/tropical methods give exact solution counts over F_q (Ax–Katz divisibility of point counts) and might give mod-2 parity of solution counts.
first_step: Compute #U_n(F_q) exactly via the toric model and check Ax–Katz-type q-divisibility; record whether any parity information survives to positive integer points.

title: Hidden Number Problem formulation: recover/obtain A from partial information on A·x mod p
connection: Boneh–Venkatesan's HNP finds α from approximations of α·t_i mod p. The ES₅ condition r(p/A) = 3 says A/p lies near 1/v with a prescribed error structure (A = (p+u)/v), an approximation statement about A mod p.
why: HNP and lattice-reduction tools are native for 'find an element mod p with given approximate multiples'. Reversing them (choose A with small multiples) is a geometry-of-numbers existence question.
first_step: Write the ES₅ word condition as 'vA ≡ u (mod p) with uv small, (u,v) in a hyperbolic region'; check the Minkowski bound for the lattice {(x, y) : y ≡ Ax mod p} restricted to non-residue A.

title: The lattice Λ_A = {(x,y) : y ≡ Ax (mod p)}: ES₅ ⇔ a non-residue A whose lattice has a short vector in a hyperbolic region
connection: vA ≡ u (mod p) with v | p+u means (v, u) ∈ Λ_A with uv small. By Minkowski every Λ_A has a vector with |x||y| ≤ p. ES₅ needs (v, u) with vA − u = p exactly (not just mod p) and positive.
why: It is geometry of numbers in its native form: minima of the family of lattices Λ_A over A ∈ QNR. Successive minima of Λ_A relate to CF data, with a Hecke-type averaging over A.
first_step: For p < 10⁵ compute λ₁(Λ_A) for all A and the minimum over non-residue A of the product-norm minimum; relate to λ(p).

title: Klein polygons / sails of the cone for p/A: HJ length = number of sail vertices
connection: The HJ digits of p/A are read off the boundary of the convex hull of the non-zero lattice points in the cone of the toric model of 1/p(1,A) (e.g. cone((0,1),(p,−A)) up to orientation convention; Klein's sail). The boundary lattice points are the HJ convergents (r(p/A) + 2 Hilbert-basis points), and geometric vertices are the points with digit ≥ 3. So r(p/A) = 3 means exactly 3 interior boundary points.
why: Arnold's statistics of sails and multidimensional continued fractions are a native toolbox. Sails with few vertices are rare and structured.
first_step: Express 'sail of cone(p,A) has 3 interior vertices' and count over A ∈ QNR; compare with Arnold's predictions for random cones.

title: Subconvexity for L(1/2, f × χ_{−4p}) and shrinking-target CM equidistribution
connection: Equidistribution of CM points in shrinking targets reduces (via Waldspurger) to subconvexity for twisted L-functions. ES certificates live in a target of measure ~p^{−1/2+o(1)}.
why: It gives the precise exponent gap: Weyl-strength subconvexity yields shrinking targets of size p^{−1/12}-ish, far from p^{−1/2}. It is a clean calibration.
first_step: Compute the target measure exactly, then the required subconvexity exponent; record the gap.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL₂ (Publ. IHES 2010)

title: Smith theory / ℤ/2-equivariant topology: fixed points of an involution on a ℤ/2-acyclic certificate complex
connection: Smith theory: an involution on a mod-2 acyclic finite complex has a non-empty mod-2 acyclic fixed set. A simplicial complex on solutions (or near-solutions) that is provably ℤ/2-acyclic, with an involution whose fixed points are certificates, would give existence.
why: It is the topological generalisation of 'odd number of fixed points', more flexible than plain parity because acyclicity can be proved by shellability or discrete Morse theory.
first_step: Define a complex on words of all p′ ≤ p (or on near-certificates) with faces from shared letters; compute mod-2 homology for small p.

title: Discrete Morse theory / matching on the poset of near-solutions
connection: Acyclic matchings on a poset (Forman) count critical cells, and Euler characteristic = alternating count of critical cells. If an ES-defined poset has Euler characteristic ≠ 0, a critical cell (certificate) must exist.
why: It is a combinatorial-topology tool that generalises sign-reversing involutions with a global acyclicity condition, a strictly richer version of the windmill route.
first_step: Define a poset of partial certificates (e.g. levels/divisor pairs ordered by divisibility) and compute its Euler characteristic as a function of p (small p).
refs: Forman, Morse theory for cell complexes (1998)

title: Lefschetz number of a map on a 'certificate space' with ES-certificate fixed points
connection: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem: L(f) ≠ 0 ⇒ fixed point. A continuous or algebraic self-map of a compact space whose fixed points are ES certificates and whose Lefschetz number is computable would prove existence.
why: It is the classic topological existence engine; the windmill is its discrete special case. A finite-field version (Lefschetz trace for Frobenius) counts points over F_q, not integral points.
first_step: Record the attempts in invol_topological.md; look for algebraic maps on U_n's compactification whose fixed loci are positive points (e.g. the cyclic permutation composed with a birational involution).

title: q-deformed rationals [p/A]_q (Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko) and Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links
connection: MGO's q-rationals have numerator polynomials with positive coefficients, which equal (up to normalisation) Jones polynomials of 2-bridge links (Kogiso–Wakui). The fan graph is the Tait graph, so the Jones polynomial is a Tutte specialisation. ES₅ concerns the class of A, i.e. which 2-bridge link has numerator p.
why: A root-of-unity specialisation detecting (A/p) would make the ES sign a quantum invariant with positivity structure (q-rationals), possibly giving inequalities.
first_step: Compute [p/A]_q numerators for p < 300 and evaluate at q = i, e^{iπ/4}, e^{2πi/8}; test whether any evaluation's phase equals (A/p) on words.
refs: Morier-Genoud–Ovsienko, q-deformed rationals and q-continued fractions (Forum Math. Sigma 2020; check)

title: Divisor class group of the toric ring k[σ^∨ ∩ M] ≅ ℤ/p and the canonical class: the sign as an Atiyah–Bott/Gorenstein index datum
connection: The cyclic quotient 1/p(1,A) has class group ℤ/p generated by a boundary divisor D₁. The canonical class K corresponds to −(1 + A)·[D₁]-type data, so the 'position of K in ℤ/p' is a quadratic-residue question about 1 + A or A.
why: Native singularity invariants (Gorenstein index, canonical class position) are computable and might rephrase the sign as 'K is a square multiple of a generator'.
first_step: Compute [K] ∈ Cl = ℤ/p for 1/p(1,A) and express its square class via A; compare with (A/p).

title: Arithmetic topology (Morishita): Legendre symbol as mod-2 linking number of prime knots
connection: In arithmetic topology (q/p) is the mod-2 linking number of 'prime knots' p and q in Spec ℤ. (A/p) = Σ_q v_q(A) lk(p,q) mod 2, and Rédei symbols are Milnor triple-linking numbers. ES₅ asks p to link oddly with the 'certificate link' of some word.
why: The dictionary might suggest topological constructions (Seifert surfaces = genus-theory objects) that force an odd linking. Speculative, but categorically sound.
first_step: Read Morishita, Knots and Primes ch. 4–8; translate the slot lemma into linking-number language and see whether a Seifert-surface argument suggests a certificate.

title: Lattice-based crypto SIS/LWE hardness as a heuristic for certificate existence in relation lattices
connection: The relation lattice Λ_q(S) = {x : ∏ g_s^{x_s} = 1} is an SIS-type lattice. Its short vectors relate to subset products hitting targets. Crypto worst-case to average-case reductions say random such lattices have short vectors of predictable length (Gaussian heuristic).
why: Gaussian-heuristic predictions for short vectors give a model of certificate existence that respects lattice structure, more refined than Poisson.
first_step: Compare the Gaussian heuristic for λ₁(Λ_q(S)) with actual values for q < 10⁵, S = first k primes; quantify the deviation.

title: Braid group B₃ lift of γ_w and link invariants of its closure
connection: SL₂(ℤ) is a quotient of B₃ (B₃ → SL₂(ℤ), kernel generated by (σ₁σ₂)⁶). Lifting γ_w to a braid and closing gives a link L_w. Link invariants (signature, Jones at roots of unity) are then functions of the word.
why: It gives another topological carrier of words, different from the 2-bridge/plumbing one, with Burau/Jones machinery.
first_step: Lift γ_w via M(b) ↦ σ₁^b σ₂^{−1}-type words; compute the signature of closures for p < 200 and compare with the sign.

title: Torus-equivariant localisation: counting words as fixed points of a T-action on a toric variety
connection: Lattice points in a polytope count T-fixed points / sections of line bundles (Brion, Lawrence–Varchenko). Words at fixed t are lattice points on a hyperbola, not a polytope, but at fixed (t,u) the v-condition is linear: the union over (t,u) is a union of 1-dim lattice point sets in progressions.
why: Equivariant localisation gives exact counts with signs (via Brion's formula) and might give a closed form for weighted word counts.
first_step: Write Σ_{words} x^t y^u z^v as a sum of rational generating functions (Brion-type) for each (t,u) cone; examine the analytic structure of the full sum.

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo: rank-1 lattice rules with generator A and HJ length 3 as 'worst' lattices
connection: A 2-D rank-1 lattice rule {(k/p, kA/p)} has quality governed by the partial quotients of A/p (Zaremba index; Niederreiter). HJ length 3 with huge digits means a very bad lattice rule. ES₅ asks for a bad lattice rule with a QNR generator.
why: QMC has existence theorems for good lattice rules for all p (Korobov) and explicit constructions for prime powers (Niederreiter). The extremal-bad side with a character condition is a dual question.
first_step: Formulate ES₅ in QMC terms: ∃ QNR A such that the lattice rule has a lattice point (v, u) with uv small and vA − u = p (the dual lattice has a very short vector). Compare with Korobov averaging over A ∈ QNR.
refs: Niederreiter, Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods (1992)

title: Toric log del Pezzo / weighted projective planes from Egyptian triples (Nill–Kasprzyk dictionary)
connection: Unit-fraction equations classify reflexive/Gorenstein toric Fano simplices (1 = Σ 1/k_i ↔ weighted projective spaces P(q₀,…) with q_i | Σq). For ES, the weights (yz, xz, xy)/g give a weighted P² whose 'index' (Σq)/lcm(q) is tied to 4/n. ES ⇔ some weighted P² has a prescribed index-type invariant.
why: The toric-Fano classification literature (Kasprzyk, Nill, Conrads) has tools for exactly 'which weight vectors satisfy divisibility conditions'. That gives a geometric home for the original Egyptian equation.
first_step: Work out the exact invariant: for P(a,b,c) with (a,b,c) ∝ (1/x,1/y,1/z), compute (a+b+c)/lcm(a,b,c) and the Gorenstein index in terms of n; check against Kasprzyk's tables of fake weighted planes.
refs: Conrads, Weighted projective spaces and reflexive simplices (2002)
Kasprzyk, Bounds on fake weighted projective space (2009; check)

title: Quantum modular forms / Ẑ-invariants of the ES Seifert spaces
connection: WRT invariants and GPPV Ẑ-invariants of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres are false-theta functions, i.e. quantum modular forms (Lawrence–Zagier for the Poincaré sphere; Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa). ES Seifert spaces M(0; 1/x,1/y,1/z) with e = −4/n form a family indexed by solutions.
why: Sum over solutions of a quantum invariant gives a generating object attached to n. Speculative, but it puts the solution set into an automorphic-adjacent structure different from Thm K.
first_step: Compute Ẑ (GPPV formula for Seifert spaces) for the ES Seifert spaces of small n and inspect the dependence on n.
refs: Gukov–Pei–Putrov–Vafa, BPS spectra and 3-manifold invariants (2017; check arXiv)
Lawrence–Zagier, Modular forms and quantum invariants of 3-manifolds (1999)

title: Hyperbolic orbifold coverings: Riemann–Hurwitz between ES triangle orbifolds of different n
connection: If S²(x,y,z) covers S²(x′,y′,z′) with degree d, then χ scales: (4/n − 1) = d(4/n′ − 1). Orbifold coverings between triangle orbifolds (Singerman's list of inclusions of triangle groups) therefore give transport between n and n′.
why: Singerman's classification of triangle-group inclusions is finite and explicit, which might give a small set of exact transport laws.
first_step: From Singerman's list, derive all relations n ↦ n′ induced by inclusions Δ(x,y,z) ⊂ Δ(x′,y′,z′); check whether any maps primes to primes.
refs: Singerman, Finitely maximal Fuchsian groups (J. LMS 1972)

title: Gauss–Bonnet / area argument: hyperbolic area of the 'certificate horoball region' vs number of words
connection: In the closed-horocycle or Farey picture, words correspond to cusp regions whose hyperbolic area can be computed by Gauss–Bonnet. Total area ≈ count × typical area gives a geometric derivation of the log²p main term.
why: A geometric derivation might reveal a monotonicity or tiling argument (regions tiling a fixed area) that forces at least one word in each 'colour' region.
first_step: Compute the hyperbolic area of the union of HJ-length-3 regions at level p and check whether it is asymptotically a constant (tiling-type) or grows.

title: Thue's lemma / short vectors in lattices L_{p,λ} producing (★) triples
connection: Thue's pigeonhole gives |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ λy (mod p). Choose λ from ES structure (e.g. λ ≡ −4⁻¹ or ratios from Rat_e) and test whether short vectors produce positive (★) data.
why: Pigeonhole-in-a-box is the cheapest every-p mechanism; ES's linear congruence p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) has a modulus depending on the unknowns, so a 2-D lattice must be found for each candidate level.
first_step: For fixed C (or u), (★) says 4uC − 1 | p + u: build the lattice {(x,y) : x ≡ y·λ_C mod (something)} and check numerically whether LLL-short vectors give solutions.

title: Small vector + congruence ⇒ equality, for the cubic ES polynomial (Ankeny-style)
connection: Thue/Ankeny: if F(v) ≡ 0 mod M and |F(v)| < M then F(v) = 0. For F = 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with |v| ≈ X: |F| ≈ pX² and Minkowski gives |v| ≈ M^{1/3}; the scales match when M ≳ p³, X ≈ p.
why: The scale bookkeeping does not immediately fail; the open question is whether an affine sublattice of index ~M on which F ≡ 0 (mod M) exists.
first_step: Classify affine sublattices of ℤ³ on which F vanishes mod q for primes q (e.g. the Type II slices y,z ≡ 0 mod p); see if CRT combinations of such slices reach M ≳ p³.

title: Multiscale induction on level sizes
connection: Wang–Zahl proved 3D Kakeya by multiscale induction (sticky structure). ES certificates live at scales (C, u, B) with uBC ≈ p/4; formulate a statement S(X): 'every p has a certificate with C ≤ X or a structural reason to have one at scale X²' and attempt an induction on scales.
why: Scale induction is how several every-type geometric statements were proved recently; ES has a natural scale hierarchy.
first_step: From data, record for each p the smallest C with a certificate and the 'near miss' structure at smaller C; look for a recursive pattern across dyadic scales.
refs: arXiv:2502.17655 (Wang-Zahl, Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions)

title: Topological existence: Tucker/Ky Fan on a complex built from divisor lattices
connection: Lovász proved Kneser via Borsuk–Ulam; Tucker's lemma is its combinatorial form. Build a simplicial complex from divisor configurations of 4Cp+1 across levels with a free ℤ/2-action (d ↔ N/d swap or u ↔ B swap) such that an equivariant labelling without a 'complementary edge' is impossible, and complementary edges are certificates.
why: Topological methods give existence with no counting at all, immune to the polylog-main-term problem.
first_step: Toy version: for one level C, model divisors as vertices of a cross-polytope (±q_i) and check whether certificate-freeness defines an antipodal-free labelling; compute its index.

title: Weak subconvexity: ES needs only an ε-saving over the trivial bound R ≥ 0
connection: Soundararajan's weak subconvexity extracts a (log)^{−δ} saving from multiplicativity and mean values alone. ES: R = M_gen + X with X ≥ −M_gen trivially (R ≥ 0); ES is exactly 'X > −M_gen', any saving over the trivial bound. Seek a multiplicativity-driven argument producing X ≥ −(1 − δ)M_gen.
why: Frames ES as the weakest possible improvement over a trivial bound, the regime where 'soft' multiplicative arguments sometimes succeed.
first_step: Identify the multiplicative structure of the coefficients in X(p) (characters of order ≥ 3 mod 4uB evaluated at p) and test whether a Halász-type mean-value argument applies.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: Family of twists by characters mod p: R as a coefficient of a p-twisted object
connection: Subconvexity in the q-aspect uses the family of all characters mod q. ES at p involves characters mod p evaluated at small integers ((−m/p) in T(p)); consider the family {R_χ(p) : χ mod p} of character-twisted certificate counts and its moments, where orthogonality mod p is available.
why: The q-aspect family is the natural family for a fixed p (it does not need varying p), so moment methods apply without leaving p.
first_step: Define R_χ(p) = Σ_{certificates} χ(u)… for χ mod p; compute Σ_χ |R_χ(p)|² exactly by orthogonality and see whether it controls the trivial-character term.

title: Meta: build the dividing-line table as a feature matrix and fit a decision tree
connection: Encode each catalog problem by features (count order, obstruction type, witness type, rigidity, reservoir, periodic parameter, symmetry group) and outcome; fit a tiny decision tree and see where ES lands and which feature flips it.
why: A crude but systematic way to read off the dividing line from data; the splits are candidate 'missing features'.
first_step: Export catalog tags from data/z52b/dividing.jsonl to a CSV, hand-correct features, fit sklearn DecisionTreeClassifier with depth ≤ 3.

title: Exceptions are about dispersion, not mean: squarefree-ES (mean 19.8) has 3 exceptions, 20/p (mean 26.4) has 60 still occurring at 9·10⁴
why: Families defined as a 'share' of all solutions (squarefree, lcm-closed, no-3) inherit U's tight distribution and have tiny exception sets; families defined by a multiplicative constraint (k | xyz, the (★) line) have heavy lower tails. For a proof, pick families of the first kind.
first_step: Measure the coefficient of variation of each family's count (residual after log p) and plot last-exception vs CV; test the predicted monotone relation.

title: OEIS has 2026 ES entries (A392469, A397366, A396825, A400619) — active outside community
connection: Four ES-related sequences were added in 2026 by Gold, van Tol, Witteveen, plus Alekseyev's A287116 (2017); the campaign's hard-prime lists and our variant failure sets are absent.
why: The OEIS ES cluster is an active, low-cost outreach channel; contributing the R-zeros, U failures, I3 zeros, lcm-closed/no-3/squarefree exceptions and the isosceles law would connect to these authors' searches (e.g. Witteveen searched to 4·10¹¹).
first_step: Prepare a batch of 6–8 submissions with b-files and cross-references to A139665, A392469, A400619, A287116.

title: Hardness vs the order of 10 mod p (decimal period) — category check
connection: Decimal period of 1/p is ord_p(10); a correlation would only reflect (2/p), (5/p) structure already captured.
why: Guards against 'recreational' fingerprints; if a residual correlation remains after controlling for (2/p), (5/p), that is a genuine surprise.
first_step: Partial Spearman of U-residual with ord_p(10)/(p−1) given (2/p), (5/p).

title: Polynomial recurrence selectors
connection: Ask whether a parameter sequence chosen by polynomial recurrence repeatedly enters a sufficient residue pattern.
why: Recurrence could replace an unstructured search if its visits can be made effective.
first_step: Choose one exact sufficient congruence pattern and compute visits of quadratic parameter sequences modulo its modulus.

title: CRT covering radius
connection: View simultaneous modular exclusions as a periodic subset of integers and ask about its largest parameter gap.
why: The largest gap directly measures how far an auxiliary search may have to travel.
first_step: For several small modulus sets, enumerate the allowed residues over one period and compute maximum gaps.

title: Epsilon-net search portfolios
connection: Ask whether a small portfolio can hit every sufficiently large witness set in a specified finite parameter universe.
why: An epsilon-net statement would be a finite search guarantee, not a proof for all primes without uniform hypotheses.
first_step: Define the witness-set universe for a bounded experiment and compare greedy nets with random samples.

title: Discrepancy-balanced family splits
connection: Color certificate families into two portfolios whose coverage counts stay close across sampled primes.
why: Balanced splits can reveal genuine diversity and create independent-looking diagnostic datasets.
first_step: Solve a small discrepancy-minimization problem on the family-prime incidence matrix.

title: Rewriting confluence
connection: Orient exact identity transformations and ask whether different reduction paths reach a common normal form.
why: Confluence would make duplicate removal and family comparison mathematically cleaner.
first_step: For a finite rule set, enumerate critical overlaps and check equality by cross multiplication.

title: Learning the next family to try
connection: Predict which exact certificate family should be attempted first from cheap features of p.
why: A learned selector accelerates search without becoming part of the correctness argument.
first_step: Compare a small classifier with a fixed family order using measured total arithmetic operations.

title: Sylvester-style product recurrences
connection: Check how classical product recurrences for Egyptian fractions encode divisibility, then ask whether alternative initial conditions yield three-term terminal states.
why: Product recurrences provide exact rational identities whose length and congruences can be tracked.
first_step: Locate a reliable source for the recurrence, derive it independently, and test modified initial parameters symbolically.

title: Primary-source identity genealogy
connection: Trace an elementary ES identity backward through citations to learn which substitutions and failed variants accompanied it.
why: Historical derivations may reveal nearby constructions omitted from modern summaries.
first_step: Choose one commonly reproduced identity, locate its earliest accessible source, and record the original parameter restrictions.

title: Lemma barter across communities
connection: Package one arithmetic lemma and one potentially useful external theorem hypothesis as a two-way translation task for specialists.
why: The exchange can expose a missing hypothesis or a tractable substitute without asking for a verdict on ES.
first_step: Draft separate finite-group and quadratic-form versions of one concrete subproblem, each with a worked example and an explicit desired conclusion.

title: Sylvester's 1880 sequence and Egyptian fraction 'denominator growth': why 3-term is the hard case
connection: Sylvester's greedy gives 4/n in ≤ 4 terms always; the gap between 4 (easy, greedy) and 3 (open) is the whole conjecture. Historically, similar 'one fewer term' gaps were closed by divisor-structure lemmas (e.g. Nagell's results on 2/n, 3/n).
why: Revisit how the k = 2 and numerator 2, 3 cases were resolved (they are theorems); the proof pattern for 3/n (always ≤ 2 terms? no: 3/n = 2 terms iff n has a divisor ≡ 2 mod 3; else 3 terms) suggests that ES is the first case where the 'iff' divisor criterion is not local — which is exactly Mordell–Schinzel. Document the exact historical sequence of results.
first_step: Search and read: Nagell 1922/23 on a/n = 1/x + 1/y; Mordell's chapter 30; list which cases (numerator a, k terms) are theorems and by what method.

title: Rhind papyrus 2/n table: did the Egyptian scribes' decomposition rules form a covering system?
connection: The 2/n table decomposes 2/n (odd n ≤ 101) into 2–4 unit fractions by patterns depending on n's factors; scholars (Gillings, Abdulaziz) reconstructed the rules. The structure is a historical 'covering by identities' for numerator 2.
why: Recreational/historical lens; the scribes' choice of 'nice' decompositions (small, even denominators) foreshadows the modern preference for Type I/II; cheap read.
first_step: Read Abdulaziz 'On the Egyptian method of decomposing 2/n into unit fractions' (Historia Math 2008) and note whether any rule there generalises to 4/n with 3 terms.

title: Elsholtz–Tao §'open questions' list — re-audit which are now answered and which lead to ES
connection: ET 2013 list several open problems (lower bounds on f(n) for all n? distribution of Type I vs II; polynomial identities). A decade later, some may be resolved in papers not yet in the repo.
why: Cheap literature update with precise targets.
first_step: Re-read ET §1.3–1.4 'open problems'; for each, search arXiv 2013–2026 (citations of ET via Semantic Scholar) and note status.

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz / Stefan Planitzer directly what they consider the current frontier
connection: People item: the authors of the almost-all lower bound f(n) ≥ (log n)^{log 6 + o(1)} are the closest active experts; a short email with the campaign's barrier map attached could elicit either a known dead-end or a tip.
why: Human expert input is cheap relative to the search cost; the campaign's FRONTIER.md is a ready-made attachment.
first_step: Draft a 10-line email summarising the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) and asking (i) is this reduction known, (ii) any route they abandoned; send.
refs: Elsholtz–Planitzer, 'Egyptian fractions and the Erdős–Straus conjecture' (Monatsh. Math 2020?)

title: Post the single-integer lower tail as a MathOverflow question
connection: FRONTIER §2's reduction ('a specific integer tied to p must have a divisor in a class with modulus part of the solution') is a clean, citable question for MO: 'Is there any known theorem giving ≥1 divisor in a tied residue class for every n?'
why: MO has answered 'is there any theorem of shape X' questions well (experts recall obscure results); low cost.
first_step: Write the MO question with the precise statement (4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C for some C), the heuristic count log²p, and the known results (Lenstra upper bound, almost-all results); post under number-theory tag.

title: Pólya–Vinogradov-era people: ask Igor Shparlinski about divisor-restricted modular hyperbola points
connection: Shparlinski has many papers on modular hyperbolas and on divisors in residue classes; the exact ES-shaped question (points on xy ≡ −1 mod e with x,y | N) is in his wheelhouse.
why: People item; cheap; he may know a relevant character-sum bound or a reason it's hopeless.
first_step: Email with the e-slice formulation; ask whether 'hyperbola points with both coordinates dividing a given N' has been studied.

title: Mordell's chapter 30 'the equation 4/n' — the discarded alternative parametrisations
connection: Mordell lists several families beyond the mod-840 ones and remarks on their limitations; the discarded families may be non-polynomial in disguise.
why: Primary-source check; the campaign cites Mordell via secondary literature.
first_step: Read Mordell ch. 30 fully; transcribe every identity and its residue class; compare with the repo's identity census (git grep -il 'identit' -- 'DISCOVERIES.md').

title: Erdős's 'covering congruences' letters and the Erdős–Selfridge sign heuristics as hints for which modulus families to try
connection: Erdős proposed many covering-type conjectures; his letters to Selfridge (published partially) contain rules of thumb for when covering fails; a historian's reading may give the exact reason Erdős believed ES was 'not provable by congruences alone'.
why: History-of-ideas item; cheap.
first_step: Search 'Erdős Straus conjecture congruences cannot suffice Erdős remark' and read Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' §on unit fractions for Erdős's own assessment.
refs: Erdős–Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980)

title: Games: ES as a two-player game (Adversary picks p, Prover picks C, Adversary reveals factorisation...) and its game value
connection: Formulate the proof search as a game to apply game-theoretic/learning-theoretic bounds: Prover's strategy = a (possibly adaptive) sequence of C's; Adversary = the integers. The minimal 'strategy depth' is C_min's worst case.
why: Meta-reformulation; it frames adaptive strategies (choose next C based on factorisation of 4C₁p+1) which are not covering systems — the adaptive route has been underexplored.
first_step: Design an adaptive strategy: C₁ = 1; if 4p+1 = Π q_i (all ≡ 1 mod 4), set C₂ = q₁ (a prime factor), check 4q₁p+1; etc. Test whether adaptive depth is smaller than C_min for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Category-theoretic / functorial view: ES as a natural transformation between the functors n ↦ Div(4Cn+1) and n ↦ residue classes
connection: Half-joke, half-meta: which constructions are *natural in n*? Polynomial identities are natural transformations ℤ[n] → solutions; Mordell–Schinzel says no natural transformation exists on square classes. The question becomes: what is the weakest 'naturality' (e.g. natural in the category of ℤ with Legendre-symbol decorations) that admits a solution map?
why: Organises the 'what kind of identity' question by the structure the identity is allowed to see (polynomial / Legendre symbols / factorisation of 4Cn+1 / full factorisation of n). A hierarchy of 'identity types' with the known no-go results placed on it is a useful map.
first_step: Write the hierarchy: (0) polynomial in n; (1) polynomial in n and ⌊√n⌋; (2) depending on n mod M for bounded M (= covering); (3) depending on Legendre symbols of n w.r.t. bounded primes; (4) depending on the factorisation of 4Cn+1 for bounded C; (5) unbounded. Place Mordell–Schinzel at (0), and ask which level ES's known data refutes.

title: Meta: switch the primary object from 'f(p) ≥ 1' to 'the failure set F_K = {p : no certificate with parameters ≤ K}' and study F_K as K grows
connection: F_K is a well-defined, computable set for each K; ES says ∩_K F_K ∩ primes = ∅. The sequence F_K (density, structure, smallest elements, Legendre profiles) is a richer object than f(p) and directly mirrors 'squares + sporadic' phenomena (F_∞ ⊇ odd squares).
why: Reframing from 'count' to 'nested exceptional sets' matches how Rickards–Stange and HKRS state results and may expose structure (e.g. F_K is eventually a union of thin sets).
first_step: Compute F_K for K = 1..50 (parameter = c²d or C) on n ≤ 10⁶ (all n); plot density vs K; list the structure of F_50.

title: Meta: crowd-source via Polymath-style wiki a 'census of all known identities with their residue scope'
connection: Mordell, Salez, Cao–Xu (56 families), repo identity census: there is no unified machine-readable list. A JSON file (family, parameters, residue classes covered, type) enables all covering/complement computations in seconds.
why: Foundational tooling; the Cao–Xu 56 families (unverified) can be machine-verified in the process.
first_step: Parse Cao–Xu 2610.32302's families into JSON; verify each symbolically (sympy) and compute the union of residue classes mod 840·k covered.

title: Puzzle: 'three resistors/three lenses' puzzle submissions to recreational columns (Gardner, Dudeney) — any that is ES in disguise with a slick solution for a sub-case?
connection: Dudeney-style puzzles on 'divide a quantity into three unit-fraction parts' exist; a slick trick for a sub-case (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3) might be an identity not in Mordell's list.
why: Low probability, cheap.
first_step: Search 'Dudeney unit fractions three' and 'Gardner Egyptian fractions 4/n'; skim.

title: Mathematical-olympiad lens: known olympiad problems 'show 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z for n ≡ r mod m' and their solutions as identity sources
connection: Many olympiad/Putnam problems ask for specific residue classes (e.g. n ≡ 2 mod 3, n ≡ 3 mod 4); their solutions are identities already in Mordell's list, but the *techniques* (e.g. choosing x = (n+1)/2…) occasionally differ.
why: Cheap; the AoPS archive is searchable.
first_step: Search AoPS for 'Erdős–Straus' and '4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z'; collect all identities; diff against the repo census.

title: Obláth 1950 and Rosati 1954: the earliest 'verification + identities' papers — what verification method did they use and did they note hard residues?
connection: Obláth verified ES up to 10⁶-ish (1950) and Rosati extended identities; these early papers sometimes list 'residues that required special treatment' — an early version of the Mordell-hard classes.
why: Cheap history check for lost identities.
first_step: Fetch Obláth, 'Sur l'équation diophantienne 4/n = 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ + 1/x₃' (Mathesis 1950) and Rosati (Boll. UMI 1954); list identities.

title: Guy's 'Unsolved Problems in Number Theory' D11 entry: the exhaustive reference list and the 'related problems' (e.g. 5/n, a/n, Sierpiński) as a lead map
connection: Guy's UPINT D11 lists ES with ~50 references and related variants; a systematic pass over each reference for 'method' rather than 'result' is cheap and might surface forgotten approaches (e.g. Bernstein's 1962 Crelle paper, Yamamoto, Terzi).
why: Standard but possibly skipped by the campaign's literature lanes (which focused on 2024–26 arXiv).
first_step: Open UPINT 3rd ed. D11; for each reference not in LITERATURE_2026.md, note method in one line.
refs: Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, D11

title: Terzi 1971 / Bernstein 1962: the 'all n ≤ 10⁸' era used a different parametrisation (4/n = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c with a | n…) — check for a mechanism not in Type I/II language
connection: Bernstein's Crelle paper 'Zur Lösung der diophantischen Gleichung m/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z' treats general m; his parametrisation for m = 4 may differ from Elsholtz–Tao's and contain additional identity families.
why: Primary-source check.
first_step: Obtain Bernstein, J. reine angew. Math. 211 (1962); transcribe parametrisation and identities.

title: Community: write up the C-form exceptional primes + QNR lemma as a short arXiv note / MO question to invite elementary explanations
connection: The observations (C-form strictly weaker than ES; four exceptional primes below 20000 with no certificate to C = 60000; every certificate divisor is a QNR mod p) are elementary and crisp — ideal for an MO question 'Why does 409 have no factorisation 4C·409 + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C?'
why: Crowd-sourced elementary number theory is strong at exactly this kind of question; a quick answer would either kill a sub-conjecture (local obstruction) or reveal a mechanism.
first_step: Verify the four exceptions independently (Pari), extend to 10⁶ for the list, then post on MO with the QNR lemma.
