title: Prize/competition: propose ES-adjacent sub-problems (C-form exceptions; d ≤ 3 Type I coverage; one-parameter dimension) as AI-math benchmark tasks (e.g. for Epoch's FrontierMath / AIMO-like) to attract compute and attention
connection: The campaign's sub-problems are well-posed, verifiable, and open — the exact profile sought by AI-math benchmark builders; inclusion brings many independent attempts.
why: Meta/community lever; cheap.
first_step: Write three one-paragraph problem statements with verification scripts; submit to a benchmark or post as 'open sub-problems' on the Erdős problems site discussion.

title: Teaching lens: the cleanest 'why ES is hard' demo is p = 409 — build a one-page explainer and use it to brief new lanes/boards
connection: 409 is small enough to hand-check: every 4C·409 + 1 for C ≤ 10 can be factored by hand, each failure explained; yet 16·409 + 1 = 6545 = 5·7·11·17 has the c=2 Type II certificate 7·935 (7 ≡ 935 ≡ −1 mod 8). It shows the congruence-slack of c ≥ 2 concretely.
why: Improves future lane quality (shared concrete example); near-zero cost.
first_step: Write BRAINSTORM/example_409.md with the table of 4C·409+1, C ≤ 12, factorizations, residues mod 4C, and the c=2 rescue.

title: Ask on the Lean Zulip (#maths) and Terence Tao's blog whether anyone has tried to formalise ES partial results or has unpublished ES notes
connection: Tao co-authored the key counting paper and writes about Erdős problems; the Zulip community has formalised Egyptian-fraction results (Bloom–Mehta). A short, specific question about the single-integer lower tail (FRONTIER §2) might get a comment from Tao or Bloom.
why: People lever; cheap.
first_step: Post a concise question in Zulip #maths (and as a comment on a relevant blog post) with the exact statement and the C-form exception data.

title: Meta: hand the C-form/Type I c=1 exceptional-set program to a dedicated lane — it is cheap, concrete, and produces test cases regardless of outcome
connection: The program: (i) census to 10⁶–10⁷ of both one-parameter exceptional sets; (ii) forced-symbol discovery; (iii) obstruction proofs for 409 and 2521; (iv) disjointness conjecture; (v) OEIS + MO publication.
why: Of all items in this lane these have the best ratio of concreteness to novelty; the outcome calibrates the whole 'one-parameter vs two-parameter' question.
first_step: Write a one-page brief for a follow-up lane with the five steps and the scripts to start from.

title: Erdős–Graham book 'Old and new problems' chapter on unit fractions as a map of solved/unsolved
connection: Erdős–Graham (1980) list dozens of unit-fraction problems; several since solved (Croot, Bloom, Martin) ↔ ES.
why: Each solved neighbour gives a method; an indexed table 'problem → method → why it fails for ES' extends the z52 dossier cheaply.
first_step: Pull every unit-fraction problem from erdosproblems.com with status 'proved' and record the key method in one line each.

title: Tao's 2011 blog post comment thread as a mine of unexplored ideas
connection: Tao's blog post on the Elsholtz–Tao paper drew comments with heuristic and computational ideas ↔ campaign may not have harvested all.
why: Cheap source of community-generated angles that were never followed up.
first_step: Read the comments on terrytao.wordpress.com 2011/07 'On the number of solutions to 4/p = …' and extract each distinct idea into this list.

title: Ahmadi–Bleicher and 'exceptional set has measure zero' line as an independent history thread
connection: Several 1990s–2000s results counted ES solution sets on average ↔ ET 2013.
why: Cheap literature completeness check; may contain a technique (e.g. Bleicher's construction) the campaign lacks.
first_step: Search MathSciNet/zbMATH for 'Erdős–Straus' 1990–2010 and list techniques per paper.

title: Erdős's 1950 paper 'Az 1/x1+…+1/xn = a/b egyenlet egész számú megoldásairól' original motivation
connection: Original Hungarian paper where ES appears ↔ what Erdős believed the method should be.
why: Historical intent sometimes contains a suggested approach never followed up.
first_step: Locate a translation or summary of Erdős 1950 (Mat. Lapok 1) and record Erdős's own heuristic.

title: Guy's UPINT D11 bibliography completeness sweep
connection: UPINT D11 lists references on ES and related unit-fraction problems ↔ repo LITERATURE_2026.md.
why: Cross-checking a canonical bibliography against the repo's literature file is cheap and catches missed classics.
first_step: Get UPINT D11 references and diff with LITERATURE_2026.md.

title: Mechanical analogy: springs in series (compliance adds) and integer stiffness
connection: Springs in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_i ↔ same algebra as resistors; equivalent reformulation.
why: Duplicate of resistor item in algebra but different community (mechanics puzzles); keep as outreach variant.
first_step: Combine with resistor outreach note (no separate work).

title: Erdős Problem #242 page and its forum/issue threads as a community channel
connection: erdosproblems.com lists ES as Problem 242 ↔ repo findings (T1 dictionary, BM main term, I3_𝒞) could be posted as remarks/partial results.
why: Problem pages attract the active AI+Lean community; precise 'what is known / what fails' notes prevent duplicated effort and invite targeted help on sub-problems.
first_step: Read erdosproblems.com/242 and its comments; draft a short factual comment listing the repo's sharpest PROVED/CERTIFIED items with pointers (subject to user approval before posting).

title: Ask Christian Elsholtz which ideas he tried and abandoned
connection: Elsholtz (Graz) co-authored ET 2013 and many unit-fraction papers ↔ unpublished negative results.
why: Experts' graveyard of failed approaches is the cheapest way to avoid repeats and may contain half-working ideas.
first_step: Draft a concise email (for the user to send) asking about abandoned approaches to pointwise ES and about the k=0 fibre of the pencil S_{n,k}.

title: MathOverflow question: 'pointwise every-n theorems with polylog expected count'
connection: The campaign's meta-finding (no known every-n theorem with polylog main term and no averaging) ↔ MO community may know counterexamples.
why: A single counterexample theorem would be a method precedent; a well-posed MO question is cheap and high-information.
first_step: Draft MO question: 'Examples of theorems proving existence for every n of an object whose expected count is polylog(n), without averaging?' with ES as motivation.

title: MathOverflow question: the shift form 'p + B has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4B for some B'
connection: Clean elementary restatement of (★) (checked numerically) ↔ community may recognise it from other contexts.
why: Elementary restatements sometimes ring bells in other subcommunities (e.g. combinatorics of consecutive integers).
first_step: Draft the MO post with the 14 known (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ as data, clearly flagging that (★) is a sufficient condition not ES itself.

title: Polymath-style open collaboration on a bounded sub-problem (e.g. 4^s + 297 family)
connection: Polymath projects (Tao, Gowers) solved bounded problems by crowd effort ↔ open thin families in repo.
why: A well-scoped, verifiable target with computational components suits crowd/AI collaboration.
first_step: Write a one-page 'problem statement + known techniques' for 4^s + 297 and 15·2^s + 1 suitable for an open call.

title: Conference targeting: present T1 dictionary / BM main term at a unit-fraction or Diophantine meeting
connection: Talks at e.g. 'Rational points' workshops or Integers conference ↔ feedback from algebraic geometers on the pencil theorem.
why: Expert feedback is the missing external review; repo results are internally reviewed only.
first_step: List upcoming 2027 workshops on rational/integral points (e.g. 'Rational Points' series) and identify one where a short talk/poster fits; prepare abstract.

title: External referee review of the 'Type I sum ≪ N log² N unconditional' note
connection: Repo's Elsholtz–Tao log-log removal claims need expert scrutiny ↔ submitting to a journal or arXiv.
why: Turning internal results into refereed ones raises their value and might attract experts to ES.
first_step: Identify the most self-contained note (paper/es-typei-heegner-note) and prepare it for arXiv submission per user approval.

title: Reorganise search: 'barrier-first' dataset of every approach × which step fails, as a public table
connection: Repo's barriers B1–B9 ↔ a public, structured negative-results database prevents others from repeating.
why: Negative results are under-published; a curated table is a community service and clarifies what remains.
first_step: Export FRONTIER §3/§4 barrier map as a CSV with (approach, step, barrier, reference) and render as a web page.

title: Meta: generate approaches by 'pairing barriers with escape hatches' systematically
connection: Each barrier theorem has stated scope; scopes have complements (hatches) ↔ enumerate hatch × thick-object pairs mechanically.
why: Systematic hatch enumeration guarantees coverage; G1 matrix is one instance.
first_step: Extract scope conditions from each barrier and generate the Cartesian product of complements; dedupe against repo memos.

title: Recreational: ES puzzle app / daily puzzle for crowd-sourced hard instances
connection: Puzzles like 'write 4/p as three unit fractions' ↔ crowd intuition on hard p.
why: Mostly outreach; humans sometimes find structured solutions faster than search for special forms of p.
first_step: Prototype a web page that gives a random hard prime and checks user answers; log solving strategies.

title: Meta: use the z52b merged list as training data for a 'connection predictor'
connection: Hundreds of connections with tags ↔ cluster and find under-explored tag combinations.
why: Tag co-occurrence analysis reveals blind spots (tag pairs never combined).
first_step: After merging lanes, compute tag co-occurrence matrix and list empty cells between high-frequency tags.

title: Meta: time-box 'wild idea sprints' with mandatory numerical kill-test on p < 10⁴
connection: Repo's drop-condition style ↔ formal protocol for testing wild items from this list cheaply.
why: Turns breadth list into actionable triage without depth bias.
first_step: Define a template: each item gets ≤ 2h, must produce a numerical test on hard primes; record pass/fail.

title: Meta: inverse literature search — who cites Elsholtz–Tao and Bright–Loughran recently
connection: Citation graph forward search ↔ new techniques applied to ES-adjacent problems since 2024.
why: Cheap way to find recent related work that keyword search misses.
first_step: Use Semantic Scholar API to list citers of arXiv:1107.1010 and 1908.02526 since 2024; skim titles.

title: Meta: survey of Chinese/Russian/Japanese-language literature on ES (e.g. Chinese journals on 4/n)
connection: Much ES-adjacent elementary work appears in non-English journals ↔ missed identities or computations.
why: Coverage check; Yamamoto's work was in Japanese journals; Chinese elementary NT journals have many unit-fraction papers.
first_step: Search CNKI-indexed titles for 'Erdős–Straus' / '4/n' and summarise any method not in repo.

title: Meta: offering a prize / bounty for sub-problems
connection: Prizes motivate community effort (Erdős prizes) ↔ well-defined sub-problems like F₁₁ or 15·2^s + 1.
why: Outreach lever; not mathematics.
first_step: Discuss with the user whether a small bounty for proving ES on 15·2^s + 1 or 4^s + 297 is desired.

title: Meta: wiki of 'equivalent forms' with conversion scripts
connection: Repo has many equivalent forms (divisor, SL₂, words, lattices, quaternions, theta) ↔ a single conversion library lets each new idea be tested in every form.
why: Lowers friction for experimentation across forms; reduces errors.
first_step: Write scripts/es_forms.py converting a certificate between all known forms with round-trip tests.

title: Meta: blind prediction contest — predict R(p) for unseen primes
connection: Forecasting competitions surface the best models of the count's fluctuation ↔ quantifies how much structure is unexplained.
why: A model achieving low error reveals structure; failure supports randomness heuristics.
first_step: Hold out primes in [10⁹, 10⁹+10⁷]; fit models on smaller p; compare RMSE of M_BM vs ML models.

title: Bernstein 1962 (Crelle) polynomial families for 4/n as historical identity catalogue
connection: L. Bernstein's 1962 paper on m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (esp. m = 4) gives families of solutions ↔ repo's identity tables.
why: Cross-check that the repo's identity catalogue includes Bernstein's families; may contain families on non-residue-class sets.
first_step: Check whether 'L. Bernstein, J. Reine Angew. Math. 211 (1962)' is the right citation and extract its families.

title: Sierpiński's 1956 monograph on decompositions into unit fractions
connection: Sierpiński 'Sur les décompositions de nombres rationnels en fractions primaires' ↔ early systematic treatment.
why: Classic sources sometimes contain lemmas or conjectures forgotten later.
first_step: Locate a scan (Mém. Soc. Math. France?) and skim for 4/n and 5/n material — check the citation first.

title: Mordell's 'Diophantine Equations' (1969) chapter on 4/n: his stated obstructions and hopes
connection: Mordell's book section where the mod-840 reduction appears ↔ his remarks on why identities can't cover squares.
why: Primary-source check of the Mordell–Schinzel narrative; might contain an overlooked suggestion.
first_step: Read the relevant section of Mordell's book and record his remarks verbatim (with page).

title: Dickson's History of the Theory of Numbers, vol. II, Egyptian-fraction chapter
connection: Dickson collects 19th-century work on unit-fraction equations ↔ pre-ES identities.
why: Cheap, may surface old parametrisations.
first_step: Skim Dickson vol. II chapter on 'sums of reciprocals' (archive.org) for equations 1/x+1/y+1/z = a/b.

title: Sylvester 1884 coin problem as the t = 1 ancestor of ES words: history link Sylvester ↔ Erdős–Straus
connection: Sylvester's Educational Times result (largest non-representable = uv − u − v) is the t = 1 case of the ES word shape tuv − u − v ↔ ES is a 'Sylvester-type' question about which primes are k-Frobenius numbers.
why: A historical bridge; the Frobenius-number literature (Ramírez Alfonsín's monograph) might have studied the inverse problem 'given n, find semigroups with g_k = n'.
first_step: Read Ramírez Alfonsín, 'The Diophantine Frobenius Problem' (OUP 2005) index for 'inverse problem' and 'k-Frobenius'; note any result on which integers are Frobenius numbers of 2-generated semigroups with multiplicity constraints.

title: Which integers are k-Frobenius numbers of ⟨u,v⟩ with k ≡ 3 (mod 4): a direct elementary question to post
connection: Restating (★) without Egyptian fractions: 'every prime p ≡ 1 (4) except 14 known ≤ 10¹⁰ is the largest integer having exactly 4C−1 representations by some coprime pair u,v'.
why: Semigroup/Frobenius community (e.g. García-Sánchez, Rosales, Ramírez Alfonsín) may recognise it; experts in that field are not in the ES network.
first_step: Draft a short note/MO post in Frobenius language with data, clearly marking that (★) is sufficient for ES but not equivalent (user approval before posting).

title: Mining the repo's ~470 brainstorm memos for dangling 'first steps' never executed
connection: Many memos end with proposed cheap tests ↔ some were never run.
why: Executing forgotten cheap tests is high-yield housekeeping.
first_step: Grep BRAINSTORM/*.md for 'first step', 'cheap test', 'TODO', 'next:' and cross-check against data/ and scripts/ for evidence of execution; list unexecuted ones.

title: Ask the LLM-board for 'connections we would be embarrassed to have missed' after merging z52b lanes
connection: Cross-model review of the merged list ↔ blind-spot detection.
why: Different models have different associative priors; a short adversarial 'what is missing' round is cheap.
first_step: After merge, run one board round with the prompt 'list 30 connections to ES absent from this list' and dedupe.

title: Odd unit-fraction solution counts and polynomial lower bounds
connection: The same MO answer cites a result giving a lower bound on the number of odd-denominator solutions for larger odd term counts, while exact counts remain unknown. This matches F04w/F12/F21/F22: a lower-bound count for constrained reciprocal representations but a gap to exact pointwise behavior.
why: The proof's construction of many solutions under a congruence restriction may transfer to lower bounds for ES representations in selected residue classes.
first_step: Read Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang, cited in the answer (arXiv:1108.6118), and extract its solution-generating operation; test whether it produces multiplicative families of ES triples.

title: Natural-proofs-style meta-barrier for ES
connection: Razborov–Rudich formalise why 'natural' combinatorial properties can't prove circuit lower bounds; the campaign's barrier theorems (B1–B9) are informal analogues for ES proof strategies.
why: A formal meta-barrier would classify proof strategies by a property (e.g. 'treats the p-tied integer as random') and prove they can't succeed against a pseudorandom model where ES fails.
first_step: Construct a random model (consistent with all known local and average facts) in which ES fails for a positive proportion of p, and list which proof techniques are 'relativising' to it.

title: Honda's count of tight contact structures on L(p,A): (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p/A = [[v,t,u]]
connection: Honda: the number of tight contact structures on L(p,q) up to isotopy is ∏(b_i − 1) over the HJ digits of p/q. So ES₅ words are lens spaces of order p with exactly three-factor tight counts in the non-square homotopy class, and I3 (letters ≥ 3) means every factor is ≥ 2.
why: Contact topology adds a natural weight (the tight-structure count) to each word. Weighted counts Σ_A ∏(b_i − 1)(A/p) might be more regular than plain counts (e.g. given by a Heegaard Floer formula).
first_step: Compute the weighted sum W±(p) = Σ_{A ∈ L₃(p), (A/p)=±1} (v−1)(t−1)(u−1) for p < 10⁵ and look for a closed form.
refs: Honda, On the classification of tight contact structures I (Geom. Topol. 2000)

title: Sparsity index: why binary Goldbach is stuck and ES is worse
connection: Binary Goldbach has a main term n/log²n among ~n terms and never got pointwise; ES has main term ≍ log²p among ≍ p log p 'trial events' (PARITY_AUDIT trial form).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from any problem ever upgraded; directs search to reformulations with denser events (fewer trials, larger main term).
first_step: Define sparsity = log(main term)/log(#trials) for each ES reformulation (★, b=1, ES₅, e-slice, I3 words) and tabulate; look for the least sparse one.

title: Euler's false conjecture: an 'obstruction class' that turned out solvable
connection: Euler believed n ≡ 2 (mod 4) had no orthogonal Latin squares; only 2 and 6 fail. Mordell-hard square classes look like an obstruction class for identities, yet ES holds there numerically. BSP's recursive constructions crossed the class barrier — look for recursive (product) constructions for ES certificates that move from easy classes into square classes.
why: Product/recursive constructions are exactly what identities (polynomial in p) cannot do; ES(n) ⇒ ES(kn) is a product construction but goes the wrong way.
first_step: Search for constructions producing certificates for p from certificates for auxiliary integers in easy classes (e.g. via the e-slice N = (p+e)/4 structure).

title: Explicit inequalities + finite check as the complete proof shape
connection: Bertrand's postulate is fully proved by an explicit inequality for n ≥ n₀ plus a hand check. For ES, collect every inequality-type sufficient condition (e.g. M_BM(p) > |X(p)| bound, Lagrange-pigeonhole ratio > 1 for some e, single-prime certificate count ≥ 1) and see if any admits an explicit lower-bound/upper-bound argument for all p ≥ p₀ with p₀ ≤ 10¹⁸.
why: Forces each mechanism to be phrased as an inequality between explicit quantities — useful even if none closes.
first_step: Write the 5 most promising sufficient conditions as explicit inequalities and evaluate both sides numerically at p ~ 10¹⁸ for the adversarial primes.

title: Computability world: ES for 'computable reals'/Turing degrees — category error check
connection: Considered: 'ES over computable reals' is meaningless (no integrality). Kept only the meaningful variant: ES restricted to n in a decidable set is decidable for each n, and the set of ES-failures is co-c.e.
why: Confirms nothing beyond the Π₁ item; record to avoid revisiting.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Greedy-in-a-different-order world: choose z first (largest), then solve the 2-term problem
connection: Reverse greedy: pick z among divisors-structured candidates and check if 4/p − 1/z is a 2-term sum. Different search orders define different canonical solutions and different 'certificate complexity' measures.
why: If some order gives bounded search depth for all p tested, it suggests the right certificate measure for a proof.
first_step: Implement reverse search with z ∈ {p·d : d | small numbers} and measure depth needed for p < 10^6.

title: Feature: independence of witness events
connection: Dividing-line feature 'independence of witness events'. ES UNCLEAR: certificate families share the integer p, correlations not controlled. To supply it one could: measure empirically the pairwise correlation between Type I families (a,d) and (a',d') as events over p, and bound them by large-sieve arguments
why: Crocker-type failures exploit strong correlation; Poisson heuristics need weak correlation.
first_step: Compute the covariance matrix of the 50 most frequent certificate families over p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^7.

title: Independence heuristic predicts unbounded Vmin; data show a plateau at 116 — test it
connection: If fail_v events at a prime were independent with P(fail_v) ≍ C_v(log p)^{−1/2}, the probability that all v ≤ 116 fail is tiny but the number of primes is huge; compute the expected number of primes ≤ X with Vmin > 116 under the model and compare with 0 observed.
why: A discrepancy would quantify positive dependence/repulsion between shifts (FRONTIER's joint-failure discussion) using a sharp observable.
first_step: Use the single-shift law constants from EXSET_SHIFT_DIVISORS §2 to compute E#{p ≤ 3·10⁶ : Vmin(p) > V} for V = 31, 87, 116.

title: Logarithmic weights tuned to rare witnesses
connection: Weight certificates by divisor size or auxiliary complexity to reduce domination by primes with many easy witnesses.
why: A better weight may make sparse cases more visible in moment calculations.
first_step: Compare unweighted counts with reciprocal-divisor and inverse-multiplicity weights on the same prime sample.

title: Base-digit automata
connection: Track a certificate equation digit by digit with carries in a fixed base.
why: Polynomial equalities admit finite carry descriptions under bounded-width restrictions, yielding concrete restricted models.
first_step: Build a base-two carry checker for bounded denominator triples and minimize its state graph.

title: Weighted automata for word height
connection: Add costs measuring coefficient size or word length to the congruence automaton.
why: Shortest accepted paths can find economical candidate certificates while respecting exact finite-state constraints.
first_step: Run shortest-path search with logarithmic coefficient cost and compare candidates against direct enumeration.

title: Synchronizing words for congruences
connection: Ask whether a shared suffix of elementary operations sends many residue states into a useful target set.
why: Such a suffix would be a reusable congruence repair mechanism, if allowed moves preserve the needed algebra.
first_step: Enumerate short suffixes in the modular transition system and measure the size of their target preimages.

title: Carry cellular automata
connection: View the multiplication and addition in the cleared ES equation as local carry interactions on digit strings.
why: Local update rules may reveal impossible digit patterns or efficient branch propagation.
first_step: Implement a bounded-width carry propagation diagram for a toy prime and compare its pruning with naive digit search.

title: Scheduling complementary searches
connection: Treat each family as a job with a measurable cost and a prime-dependent success profile.
why: Scheduling can improve exploratory reach without confusing computational efficiency with a proof.
first_step: Compare round-robin, least-cost-first, and residue-conditioned schedules on a held-out prime interval.

title: SAT encodings of bounded denominator search
connection: Encode the cleared ES equation and positivity bounds as a Boolean circuit with explicit carries.
why: A satisfying assignment is an exactly checkable finite witness, and the encoding may expose reusable logical constraints.
first_step: Build a tiny bounded instance for p=13 and compare decoded models with direct enumeration.

title: SMT over mixed integer structures
connection: Combine integer arithmetic, divisibility, and bit-vector residue constraints in a bounded solver model.
why: Different theories may cooperate better than one large expanded polynomial equation.
first_step: Model one auxiliary divisor family with explicit finite bounds and compare integer-only with mixed-theory formulations.

title: Constraint propagation on factor domains
connection: Maintain finite domains for factor residues and remove choices that cannot participate in a valid complementary pair.
why: Arc consistency can sharply reduce bounded search while preserving every actual solution.
first_step: Apply AC-3 to a three-variable factor-residue model and compare remaining domains with exhaustive solutions.

title: Proof complexity of bounded failures
connection: Compare lengths of machine-checkable unsatisfiability proofs for different bounded ES encodings.
why: Short proofs may reveal elementary exclusions worth expressing as human lemmas.
first_step: For several deliberately too-small boxes, compare proof sizes under direct and factorized encodings.

title: Trusted-kernel pipelines
connection: Route heuristic discoveries into a tiny theorem-checking kernel rather than trusting the search or symbolic algebra package.
why: The proof obligation stays explicit even when discovery uses complicated tools.
first_step: Choose one elementary family and separate its discovery script from a minimal proof of the resulting identity and divisibility conditions.

title: Algorithmic simplicity of difficult instances
connection: Compare the shortest known certificate-generating program with the smallest numerical certificate.
why: A huge denominator might still have a simple recurrence description, suggesting a different notion of difficulty.
first_step: For a small set of large-height examples, search short recurrences generating their denominator triples.

title: Parameterized complexity by factor count
connection: Treat the number of distinct auxiliary prime factors or modulus structure as an algorithmic parameter.
why: Subset-product search may be tractable in a parameter even when the integer itself is large.
first_step: Derive running-time bounds for residue selection in terms of factor count and group invariant factors.

title: Meet-in-the-middle divisor selection
connection: Split prime-power factors into two groups and match complementary target residues.
why: This is an exact algorithmic alternative to enumerating every divisor when modular inverses are handled correctly.
first_step: Implement the split for unit factors of a small auxiliary integer and handle nonunits in separate valuation strata.

title: Bitset propagation of attainable residues
connection: Represent reachable residues by bitsets and update them under each allowed factor power.
why: Bit-parallel operations can make large bounded surveys cheaper without changing the mathematics.
first_step: Benchmark bitset and set-based reachability for moduli below 1000 using the same factorizations.

title: Arithmetic-circuit complexity
connection: Compare expanded polynomial identities with compact straight-line arithmetic circuits.
why: A low-complexity circuit may expose composition structure that expansion obscures.
first_step: Represent three candidate families as circuits and count multiplication gates after common-subexpression elimination.

title: Product and remainder trees
connection: Use product trees to test many candidate divisors against many auxiliary values efficiently.
why: This supports broad experiments and may reveal unexpectedly reusable factors.
first_step: Design a memory-bounded remainder-tree pass for a small family of auxiliary values and target divisors.

title: Perfect-hash-style family isolation
connection: Use hash partitions to isolate one witness among many candidate factors, simplifying a bounded search subproblem.
why: Isolation can aid algorithm design, while an exact check prevents the hash mechanism from inventing witnesses.
first_step: Apply a small family of residue hashes to known multi-witness instances and measure isolation rates.

title: Permutation-equivariant certificate models
connection: Train predictors on unordered denominator triples using features invariant under all six coordinate permutations.
why: Respecting exact symmetry can reduce spurious distinctions in learned family structure.
first_step: Compare a symmetric feature model with a raw-coordinate baseline on canonicalized bounded certificates.

title: Lean formalization of one family
connection: Formalize one elementary rational identity together with its positivity and divisibility hypotheses.
why: A small verified example establishes the shape of proof obligations without trying to formalize the whole campaign.
first_step: Choose the simplest directly checked family and locate the Lean lemmas needed for rational field simplification.

title: Positivity proof certificates
connection: Attach explicit positive-factor decompositions to every symbolic denominator expression.
why: An algebraically correct identity can still fail as an ES construction if denominators are nonpositive.
first_step: For three candidate formulas, rewrite each denominator into products or sums whose signs follow from stated hypotheses.

title: Integer–rational coercion discipline
connection: Treat exact division as a separate proved step before moving a parametrization from integers to rational identities.
why: This prevents silent truncation or unjustified integrality in machine and human proofs.
first_step: Write a typed proof outline for one formula, marking every use of integer divisibility and rational coercion.

title: A library of divisibility transport lemmas
connection: Collect reusable lemmas carrying divisibility through substitutions, gcd cancellation, and complementary factors.
why: These small facts recur across many distinct constructions and can reduce proof friction.
first_step: Formalize or precisely state five transport lemmas needed by the residual factor-pair equivalence.

title: Certified completeness of finite enumeration
connection: Prove the ordered-denominator bounds used by an exhaustive verifier and connect them to its loop limits.
why: A witness checker proves individual successes; a completeness proof also validates bounded absence claims.
first_step: Write a proof outline linking x and y inequalities to each loop endpoint of a toy exhaustive search.

title: Extracting certificate algorithms from proofs
connection: Given a constructive family theorem, extract the parameter-to-denominator function with its domain test.
why: The extracted algorithm connects proof structure to measurable search behavior.
first_step: Take one hand-proved family and write its domain predicate and witness constructor as separate pure functions.

title: Resultants as specialization filters
connection: Use resultants to detect when specialized auxiliary factors acquire common divisors or lose coprimality.
why: The resultant supplies an explicit finite arithmetic obstruction to naive factor independence.
first_step: Compute the resultant of two polynomial denominator factors and derive which primes can divide both specializations.

title: Mahler equations for recursive selectors
connection: Check whether a digit-recursive certificate selector has a generating function satisfying a functional equation involving z and z^b.
why: A functional equation could certify a recursive pattern if the selector recursion is proved first.
first_step: For a toy digit-based family, derive the coefficient recursion and test the resulting Mahler-type equation formally.

title: Presburger/automatic-sequence test: is the set of (p, C_min(p)) k-automatic in any base?
connection: Automatic sequences and k-regular sequences are decidable by Walnut; if the first winning C (or Type I minimal c) were k-regular in p, Walnut could *prove* ES in that regime. Almost certainly not, but the negative result would be informative: it shows ES is 'non-automatic' which rules out all finite-automaton covering proofs.
why: Cheap and decisive one way or the other; connects to B1 in automaton language.
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁶, test for 2-/3-/10-regularity with a k-kernel rank test (compute subsequences C_min(k^e p + r) and check linear dependence).
refs: Shallit, 'The Logical Approach to Automatic Sequences' (Walnut)

title: Kolmogorov complexity of the solution 'script' (c,d,f) across primes
connection: For each p, encode the lexicographically first Type I/II solution as a string; measure compressibility across consecutive primes (gzip of the concatenation, or a learned model's perplexity). Low complexity = hidden rule.
why: Direct test for 'there is a simple hidden rule the campaign has not found'. Cheap.
first_step: Produce the (c,d,f) first-solution sequence for p ≤ 10⁶, compress with xz/zpaq, compare with compressibility of a surrogate random sequence with the same marginals.

title: Gradient-boosted classifier for 'p has a solution with C ≤ 10' and inspect feature importances
connection: Train a classifier on arithmetic features of p to predict whether a small-C certificate exists; if accuracy is high, the features used ARE a partial identity; if accuracy ≈ base rate, small-C solvability is 'random' w.r.t. all tested features.
why: Cheap, directly reveals structure or its absence in the bounded-C regime (the covering regime).
first_step: Features: p mod 840·k, Legendre symbols of primes ≤ 50, ω and smallest factors of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10; target: exists C ≤ 10 with a winning divisor. Train/test on p ≤ 10⁷.
